slides.title: Link the HIV diagnosis, immune assessment, and immediate clinical problem
slides.section: Link the HIV diagnosis, immune assessment, and immediate clinical problem
paragraphs: Resident core · 30–45 minutes with discussion

By the end, use the diagnostic sequence, recognize when ART can start promptly, identify an OI that changes immediate treatment or ART timing, and arrange prevention and follow-up. Three cases anchor the discussion. Detailed OI doses, maintenance criteria, newer therapies, and trial appraisals are in the advanced reference below.
A positive HIV test is the beginning of the assessment. HIV RNA, CD4 count, symptoms, medication history, and access to continuing treatment determine what needs to happen next.

slides.title: Confirm the diagnosis without missing acute infection
slides.section: Confirm the diagnosis without missing acute infection
paragraphs: Begin with a laboratory HIV-1/2 antigen-antibody test, followed by an HIV-1/HIV-2 differentiation assay when reactive. If the differentiation assay is negative or indeterminate, obtain HIV RNA to resolve possible acute infection. With a compatible recent exposure or acute retroviral syndrome, order RNA even when the screening test is negative.

Ask about recent PrEP or PEP, including long-acting agents, because antiretroviral exposure can alter testing patterns and resistance considerations. An isolated discordant result requires a deliberate repeat-testing plan, not reassurance or an unsupported permanent diagnosis.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Confirm the diagnosis without missing acute infection Begin with a laboratory HIV-1/2 antigen-antibody test, followed by an HIV-1/HIV-2 differentiation assay when reactive. If the differentiation assay is negative or indeterminate, obtain HIV RNA to resolve possible acute infection. With a compatible recent exposure or acute retroviral syndrome, order RNA even when the screening test is negative. Ask about recent PrEP or PEP, including long-acting agents, because antiretroviral exposure can alter testing patterns and resistance considerations. An isolated discordant result requires a deliberate repeat-testing plan, not reassurance or an unsupported permanent diagnosis. Collect HIV RNA, CD4, genotype, hepatitis serologies, renal/hepatic assessment, and other indicated baseline studies. Screen for symptoms suggesting an OI. These studies usually can be collected while arranging rapid ART; do not create an avoidable delay in an otherwise appropriate patient. Sources: early , baseline , initiation .

slides.title: Start a complete ART regimen and identify the exceptions
slides.section: Start a complete ART regimen and identify the exceptions
paragraphs: For most people starting ART, an integrase inhibitor with two appropriate NRTIs is a standard approach. Common examples are bictegravir/TAF/FTC or dolutegravir with TAF/FTC or TDF/FTC when suitable. Selection depends on organ function, pregnancy, resistance risk, hepatitis B, interactions, and access.

Dolutegravir/lamivudine has specific exclusions and is not an interchangeable rapid-start shortcut while hepatitis B and resistance results are unknown. HIV/HBV coinfection generally requires two HBV-active components, usually tenofovir plus FTC or 3TC, in a fully suppressive HIV regimen. Stopping HBV-active drugs can precipitate hepatitis.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Start a complete ART regimen and identify the exceptions For most people starting ART, an integrase inhibitor with two appropriate NRTIs is a standard approach. Common examples are bictegravir/TAF/FTC or dolutegravir with TAF/FTC or TDF/FTC when suitable. Selection depends on organ function, pregnancy, resistance risk, hepatitis B, interactions, and access. Dolutegravir/lamivudine has specific exclusions and is not an interchangeable rapid-start shortcut while hepatitis B and resistance results are unknown. HIV/HBV coinfection generally requires two HBV-active components, usually tenofovir plus FTC or 3TC, in a fully suppressive HIV regimen. Stopping HBV-active drugs can precipitate hepatitis. Prior long-acting cabotegravir PrEP, suspected resistance, or a complex treatment history changes the initial-regimen discussion. Review the guideline and obtain specialist input rather than assuming all treatment-naive patients have the same resistance risk. Timing matters: prompt ART is the usual approach, including during treatment of many OIs. Cryptococcal meningitis and TB meningitis require a separate timing plan because early immune recovery in the CNS can be harmful. Sources: arv , hbv , initiation .

slides.title: Start a complete ART regimen and identify the exceptions
slides.section: Start a complete ART regimen and identify the exceptions
paragraphs: Prior long-acting cabotegravir PrEP, suspected resistance, or a complex treatment history changes the initial-regimen discussion. Review the guideline and obtain specialist input rather than assuming all treatment-naive patients have the same resistance risk.

Timing matters: prompt ART is the usual approach, including during treatment of many OIs. Cryptococcal meningitis and TB meningitis require a separate timing plan because early immune recovery in the CNS can be harmful.
Sources: arv , hbv , initiation .
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Start a complete ART regimen and identify the exceptions For most people starting ART, an integrase inhibitor with two appropriate NRTIs is a standard approach. Common examples are bictegravir/TAF/FTC or dolutegravir with TAF/FTC or TDF/FTC when suitable. Selection depends on organ function, pregnancy, resistance risk, hepatitis B, interactions, and access. Dolutegravir/lamivudine has specific exclusions and is not an interchangeable rapid-start shortcut while hepatitis B and resistance results are unknown. HIV/HBV coinfection generally requires two HBV-active components, usually tenofovir plus FTC or 3TC, in a fully suppressive HIV regimen. Stopping HBV-active drugs can precipitate hepatitis. Prior long-acting cabotegravir PrEP, suspected resistance, or a complex treatment history changes the initial-regimen discussion. Review the guideline and obtain specialist input rather than assuming all treatment-naive patients have the same resistance risk. Timing matters: prompt ART is the usual approach, including during treatment of many OIs. Cryptococcal meningitis and TB meningitis require a separate timing plan because early immune recovery in the CNS can be harmful. Sources: arv , hbv , initiation .

slides.title: Use the syndrome to choose the first OI tests and treatment
slides.section: Use the syndrome to choose the first OI tests and treatment
rows: Subacute dyspnea and diffuse pulmonary opacities
Assess oxygenation; obtain an appropriate respiratory specimen for Pneumocystis testing and evaluate other pulmonary causes.
Start PCP treatment when suspicion is high. Steroids depend on hypoxemia, not the CD4 count alone.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Use the syndrome to choose the first OI tests and treatment Initial OI decisions in advanced HIV Syndrome Initial evaluation Management anchor Subacute dyspnea and diffuse pulmonary opacities Assess oxygenation; obtain an appropriate respiratory specimen for Pneumocystis testing and evaluate other pulmonary causes. Start PCP treatment when suspicion is high. Steroids depend on hypoxemia, not the CD4 count alone. Headache or meningitic symptoms Consider cryptococcus and TB; obtain serum/CSF studies and measure opening pressure when LP is safe. Cryptococcal meningitis needs combination induction therapy and active pressure management. ART is usually deferred about 4–6 weeks after antifungals start. Focal neurologic signs or brain lesions Obtain brain imaging and consider toxoplasma, lymphoma, PML, TB, and other causes. Treat a likely toxoplasma presentation while setting a response checkpoint and an alternative-diagnosis plan. Visual symptoms Arrange urgent dilated ophthalmologic examination. CMV retinitis is an organ diagnosis. Plasma CMV PCR alone neither establishes nor excludes retinitis. Fever, cytopenias, weight loss, or systemic illness Use exposure and organ findings to evaluate histoplasmosis, MAC, TB, bacterial infection, and malignancy. Get syndrome-directed cultures and antigen/tissue tests. A prophylaxis dose is not adequate treatment of disseminated disease. CD4 thresholds help prioritize possibilities but do not prove the diagnosis. Multiple infections can coexist. A worsening patient needs reassessment for treatment failure, another infection, toxicity, and IRIS. Sources: pcp , crypto , toxo , cmv , histo , mac .

slides.title: Separate primary prophylaxis, secondary maintenance, PrEP, and PEP
slides.section: Separate primary prophylaxis, secondary maintenance, PrEP, and PEP
rows: For a person not taking ART or starting ART, CD4 below 200 is an indication under the current NIH guidance. For someone already on ART, use the CD4 and viral-load criteria in the detailed table.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Separate primary prophylaxis, secondary maintenance, PrEP, and PEP Four different prevention decisions Purpose Decision anchor Primary PCP prophylaxis For a person not taking ART or starting ART, CD4 below 200 is an indication under the current NIH guidance. For someone already on ART, use the CD4 and viral-load criteria in the detailed table. Primary toxoplasma prophylaxis Toxoplasma IgG positivity plus CD4 below 100 is the usual indication. TMP-SMX can cover both toxoplasma and PCP prophylaxis. Primary MAC prophylaxis Consider at CD4 below 50 when effective ART will not start promptly or suppression is not achievable; exclude disseminated MAC first. It is not routinely needed with immediate effective ART. Secondary maintenance After an OI, use that disease’s own treatment-completion and immune-recovery criteria. Do not apply a primary-prophylaxis stopping rule automatically. PrEP Confirm HIV-negative status, match the regimen to the exposure population, and arrange the required testing and follow-up. Oral and long-acting options have different eligibility and dosing schedules. PEP After a qualifying exposure, start as soon as possible and no later than 72 hours; use a 28-day course and arrange follow-up testing. Do not wait for every baseline result before the first dose. Sustained viral suppression prevents sexual HIV transmission. Discuss this clearly while still addressing other STI prevention, immunizations, reproductive goals, and access to treatment. Sources: pcp , toxo , mac , prep , pep , uu .

rows: Consider at CD4 below 50 when effective ART will not start promptly or suppression is not achievable; exclude disseminated MAC first. It is not routinely needed with immediate effective ART.

TMP-SMX can cover both toxoplasma and PCP prophylaxis. It is not routinely needed with immediate effective ART. Secondary maintenance After an OI, use that disease’s own treatment-completion and immune-recovery criteria. Oral and long-acting options have different eligibility and dosing schedules. slides.section: Separate primary prophylaxis, secondary maintenance, PrEP, and PEP
rows: After a qualifying exposure, start as soon as possible and no later than 72 hours; use a 28-day course and arrange follow-up testing. Do not wait for every baseline result before the first dose.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Separate primary prophylaxis, secondary maintenance, PrEP, and PEP Four different prevention decisions Purpose Decision anchor Primary PCP prophylaxis For a person not taking ART or starting ART, CD4 below 200 is an indication under the current NIH guidance. For someone already on ART, use the CD4 and viral-load criteria in the detailed table. Primary toxoplasma prophylaxis Toxoplasma IgG positivity plus CD4 below 100 is the usual indication. TMP-SMX can cover both toxoplasma and PCP prophylaxis. Oral and long-acting options have different eligibility and dosing schedules. slides.title: Check delivery and interactions before declaring the regimen ineffective
slides.section: Check delivery and interactions before declaring the regimen ineffective
paragraphs: Ask whether the person has the medicines and can take them consistently. Review antacids and mineral supplements with integrase inhibitors, acid suppressants with rilpivirine, rifamycins, anticonvulsants, and all nonprescription products. Food requirements and absorption matter.

Recheck HIV RNA after treatment starts or changes according to the monitoring guideline, commonly within 4–8 weeks, and follow until suppressed. With persistent viremia, assess adherence, interactions, absorption, and resistance before changing therapy. Do not add a single active drug to a failing regimen.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Check delivery and interactions before declaring the regimen ineffective Ask whether the person has the medicines and can take them consistently. Review antacids and mineral supplements with integrase inhibitors, acid suppressants with rilpivirine, rifamycins, anticonvulsants, and all nonprescription products. Food requirements and absorption matter. Recheck HIV RNA after treatment starts or changes according to the monitoring guideline, commonly within 4–8 weeks, and follow until suppressed. With persistent viremia, assess adherence, interactions, absorption, and resistance before changing therapy. Do not add a single active drug to a failing regimen. Discharge planning should name the HIV clinician, provide uninterrupted medication access, specify pending-result ownership, and distinguish the ART, OI treatment, and prophylaxis stop or reassessment dates. Suppression is the start of ongoing preventive care. Sources: monitor , failure , interactions .

slides.title: Case 1 · A discordant diagnostic sequence
slides.section: Use three cases to identify the immediate decision
paragraphs: A symptomatic patient with a recent exposure has a reactive antigen-antibody test and a negative differentiation assay.
Discuss the next action and the finding that would change it.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Use three cases to identify the immediate decision Case 1 · A discordant diagnostic sequence A symptomatic patient with a recent exposure has a reactive antigen-antibody test and a negative differentiation assay. Discuss the next action and the finding that would change it. Discussion Obtain HIV RNA promptly to evaluate acute infection. Review PrEP or PEP exposure and arrange confirmation and linkage. Do not call this a negative HIV evaluation because the antibody differentiation test is negative. Case 2 · Low CD4 with hypoxemic pneumonia A patient with newly diagnosed HIV has CD4 42, diffuse opacities, and room-air PaO2 64 mm Hg. Discuss the next action and the finding that would change it. Discussion Evaluate for PCP and other pulmonary disease while starting appropriate therapy when suspicion is high. The oxygenation meets the steroid threshold for PCP. Plan ART within two weeks when feasible, toxicity monitoring, and secondary prophylaxis. Case 3 · Meningitis changes the ART clock A patient with advanced HIV has a positive CSF cryptococcal antigen and a high opening pressure. Discuss the next action and the finding that would change it. Discussion Start guideline-concordant antifungal induction and manage intracranial pressure with therapeutic LPs. Follow CSF cultures and drug toxicity. Defer ART approximately 4–6 weeks after antifungal initiation rather than applying the usual rapid-start rule.

slides.title: Discussion
slides.section: Use three cases to identify the immediate decision
paragraphs: Evaluate for PCP and other pulmonary disease while starting appropriate therapy when suspicion is high. The oxygenation meets the steroid threshold for PCP. Plan ART within two weeks when feasible, toxicity monitoring, and secondary prophylaxis.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Use three cases to identify the immediate decision Case 1 · A discordant diagnostic sequence A symptomatic patient with a recent exposure has a reactive antigen-antibody test and a negative differentiation assay. Discuss the next action and the finding that would change it. Discussion Obtain HIV RNA promptly to evaluate acute infection. Review PrEP or PEP exposure and arrange confirmation and linkage. Do not call this a negative HIV evaluation because the antibody differentiation test is negative. Case 2 · Low CD4 with hypoxemic pneumonia A patient with newly diagnosed HIV has CD4 42, diffuse opacities, and room-air PaO2 64 mm Hg. Discuss the next action and the finding that would change it. Discussion Evaluate for PCP and other pulmonary disease while starting appropriate therapy when suspicion is high. The oxygenation meets the steroid threshold for PCP. Plan ART within two weeks when feasible, toxicity monitoring, and secondary prophylaxis. Case 3 · Meningitis changes the ART clock A patient with advanced HIV has a positive CSF cryptococcal antigen and a high opening pressure. Discuss the next action and the finding that would change it. Discussion Start guideline-concordant antifungal induction and manage intracranial pressure with therapeutic LPs. Follow CSF cultures and drug toxicity. Defer ART approximately 4–6 weeks after antifungal initiation rather than applying the usual rapid-start rule.

slides.title: HIV care begins with a diagnosis, an immune assessment, and a durable treatment plan
slides.section: HIV care begins with a diagnosis, an immune assessment, and a durable treatment plan
paragraphs: This case-based primer is for residents and ID fellows, with an attending update pathway. The first block covers HIV diagnosis, ART, prevention, and longitudinal care. The second is a practical guide to opportunistic infections (OIs) and related infections. All cases are fictional teaching examples.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
HIV care begins with a diagnosis, an immune assessment, and a durable treatment plan This case-based primer is for residents and ID fellows, with an attending update pathway. The first block covers HIV diagnosis, ART, prevention, and longitudinal care. The second is a practical guide to opportunistic infections (OIs) and related infections. All cases are fictional teaching examples. Resident essentials Work through diagnosis, initial ART, OI recognition, and discharge planning. Allow 60-75 minutes for the core and 30-45 minutes for the OI workshop. Advanced pathway Add resistance, injectable treatment, ART timing controversies, and the original-trial discussion. Allow another 20-30 minutes. After completing this module, you should be able to Interpret discordant HIV tests and select the next diagnostic test. Select an initial ART strategy using resistance history, HBV status, organ function, and interactions. Build a syndrome-directed OI evaluation and specify treatment, ART timing, and prophylaxis. Distinguish virologic failure, treatment toxicity, another diagnosis, and IRIS. Deliver a discharge and prevention plan that preserves medication access and follow-up. Version 1.1. Clinical sources checked September 15, 2026. AI-assisted educational synthesis; faculty and pharmacy review pending. This is educational material, not an institutional protocol. Local laboratory order names, drug access, reporting, and referral pathways require confirmation.

slides.title: After completing this module, you should be able to
slides.section: HIV care begins with a diagnosis, an immune assessment, and a durable treatment plan
paragraphs: Interpret discordant HIV tests and select the next diagnostic test.
Select an initial ART strategy using resistance history, HBV status, organ function, and interactions.
Build a syndrome-directed OI evaluation and specify treatment, ART timing, and prophylaxis.
Distinguish virologic failure, treatment toxicity, another diagnosis, and IRIS.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
HIV care begins with a diagnosis, an immune assessment, and a durable treatment plan This case-based primer is for residents and ID fellows, with an attending update pathway. The first block covers HIV diagnosis, ART, prevention, and longitudinal care. The second is a practical guide to opportunistic infections (OIs) and related infections. All cases are fictional teaching examples. Resident essentials Work through diagnosis, initial ART, OI recognition, and discharge planning. Allow 60-75 minutes for the core and 30-45 minutes for the OI workshop. Advanced pathway Add resistance, injectable treatment, ART timing controversies, and the original-trial discussion. Allow another 20-30 minutes. After completing this module, you should be able to Interpret discordant HIV tests and select the next diagnostic test. Select an initial ART strategy using resistance history, HBV status, organ function, and interactions. Build a syndrome-directed OI evaluation and specify treatment, ART timing, and prophylaxis. Distinguish virologic failure, treatment toxicity, another diagnosis, and IRIS. Deliver a discharge and prevention plan that preserves medication access and follow-up. Version 1.1. slides.title: Use the testing sequence and recognize acute HIV before antibodies are fully detectable
slides.section: Use the testing sequence and recognize acute HIV before antibodies are fully detectable
paragraphs: HIV RNA reflects viral replication; CD4 count helps estimate immune vulnerability. A high CD4 count does not remove the indication for treatment, and a low CD4 count does not establish the cause of an acute illness. Acute HIV may resemble influenza, COVID-19, EBV/CMV mononucleosis, or secondary syphilis, with fever, rash, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, diarrhea, or aseptic meningitis. [1] [2]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Use the testing sequence and recognize acute HIV before antibodies are fully detectable HIV RNA reflects viral replication; CD4 count helps estimate immune vulnerability. A high CD4 count does not remove the indication for treatment, and a low CD4 count does not establish the cause of an acute illness. Acute HIV may resemble influenza, COVID-19, EBV/CMV mononucleosis, or secondary syphilis, with fever, rash, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, diarrhea, or aseptic meningitis. [1] [2] Laboratory diagnosis and the next step Finding Interpretation Next step Reactive laboratory HIV-1/2 antigen-antibody assay A screening result, not the complete diagnosis Perform HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation. Reactive screen and positive differentiation HIV established by the diagnostic algorithm Obtain HIV RNA, CD4, and baseline evaluation; arrange ART. Reactive screen and negative or indeterminate differentiation Acute HIV versus false-positive screening Obtain HIV-1 RNA. Detectable RNA supports acute HIV; repeat a new specimen when needed. If HIV-2 remains a concern, arrange HIV-2-specific evaluation. Negative screen with recent exposure and compatible illness Window-period infection remains possible Order HIV RNA and arrange repeat testing. Low-positive RNA, especially during PrEP or PEP Early infection, drug-modified infection, or false positivity Repeat antigen-antibody and RNA on a new specimen; obtain expert input. Do not dismiss the result or simply continue an inadequate treatment regimen. [1] Ask specifically about prior oral and injectable PrEP, PEP, and the last injection date. Recent antiretroviral exposure can alter both the testing pattern and the resistance risk. Use nonjudgmental language and confirm how the patient wants results communicated. HIV itself requires Standard Precautions. Add transmission-based precautions for the suspected accompanying pathogen, such as airborne precautions for pulmonary TB. [3]

slides.title: Collect baseline studies without creating an unnecessary delay in ART
slides.section: Collect baseline studies without creating an unnecessary delay in ART
rows: Diagnostic documentation; prior ART, PrEP/PEP, genotypes, interruptions, and current medication supply.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Collect baseline studies without creating an unnecessary delay in ART The first visit or inpatient consultation Task What to establish HIV status and prior treatment Diagnostic documentation; prior ART, PrEP/PEP, genotypes, interruptions, and current medication supply. Virology and immunity HIV RNA and CD4. Genotype for reverse transcriptase and protease; add integrase testing for prior CAB PrEP, INSTI treatment failure, or suspected INSTI resistance. Organ function and coinfection CBC, renal and liver testing, urinalysis, lipids; hepatitis A immunity; HBV surface antigen, surface antibody, core antibody; HCV testing with RNA when indicated. Prevention and special situations Pregnancy testing when relevant; site-specific STI testing and syphilis serology; TB screening after assessing for disease; Toxoplasma IgG and G6PD when relevant to OI prevention. HLA-B*5701 only if considering abacavir. Clinical feasibility Symptoms of CNS, pulmonary, ocular, or disseminated OI; drug interactions, swallowing and absorption, insurance/ADAP, transport, housing, mental health, substance use, and a confirmed follow-up clinician. [4] [1] [5] [6] Send specimens before ART when feasible. In a clinically suitable patient, do not wait for CD4 or genotype results to start an appropriate rapid-start regimen. If HBV results are pending, use a regimen with HBV activity. CNS cryptococcosis and TB meningitis are important exceptions to reflex immediate ART. [4] [7] [3] Advanced HIV is a prompt to look for an OI, not an instruction to send every available PCR. Choose specimens from the involved organ and identify which result would change treatment.

slides.title: Collect baseline studies without creating an unnecessary delay in ART
slides.section: Collect baseline studies without creating an unnecessary delay in ART
rows: HIV RNA and CD4. Genotype for reverse transcriptase and protease; add integrase testing for prior CAB PrEP, INSTI treatment failure, or suspected INSTI resistance.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Collect baseline studies without creating an unnecessary delay in ART The first visit or inpatient consultation Task What to establish HIV status and prior treatment Diagnostic documentation; prior ART, PrEP/PEP, genotypes, interruptions, and current medication supply. Virology and immunity HIV RNA and CD4. Genotype for reverse transcriptase and protease; add integrase testing for prior CAB PrEP, INSTI treatment failure, or suspected INSTI resistance. Organ function and coinfection CBC, renal and liver testing, urinalysis, lipids; hepatitis A immunity; HBV surface antigen, surface antibody, core antibody; HCV testing with RNA when indicated. Prevention and special situations Pregnancy testing when relevant; site-specific STI testing and syphilis serology; TB screening after assessing for disease; Toxoplasma IgG and G6PD when relevant to OI prevention. HLA-B*5701 only if considering abacavir. Clinical feasibility Symptoms of CNS, pulmonary, ocular, or disseminated OI; drug interactions, swallowing and absorption, insurance/ADAP, transport, housing, mental health, substance use, and a confirmed follow-up clinician. [4] [1] [5] [6] Send specimens before ART when feasible. In a clinically suitable patient, do not wait for CD4 or genotype results to start an appropriate rapid-start regimen. If HBV results are pending, use a regimen with HBV activity. CNS cryptococcosis and TB meningitis are important exceptions to reflex immediate ART. [4] [7] [3] Advanced HIV is a prompt to look for an OI, not an instruction to send every available PCR. Choose specimens from the involved organ and identify which result would change treatment.

slides.title: Choose an effective complete regimen and account for the exceptions
slides.section: Choose an effective complete regimen and account for the exceptions
paragraphs: HIV integrates into host DNA and persists in a reservoir that current ART does not eradicate. NRTIs and NNRTIs inhibit reverse transcription, INSTIs inhibit integration, and protease inhibitors prevent viral maturation. Ritonavir and cobicistat commonly serve as pharmacokinetic boosters; they are not interchangeable with an active drug in the regimen. Capsid and entry-directed agents have specialized roles. [8]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Choose an effective complete regimen and account for the exceptions HIV integrates into host DNA and persists in a reservoir that current ART does not eradicate. NRTIs and NNRTIs inhibit reverse transcription, INSTIs inhibit integration, and protease inhibitors prevent viral maturation. Ritonavir and cobicistat commonly serve as pharmacokinetic boosters; they are not interchangeable with an active drug in the regimen. Capsid and entry-directed agents have specialized roles. [8] For most treatment-naive adults without prior long-acting cabotegravir exposure, initial treatment uses bictegravir/TAF/FTC or dolutegravir plus two nucleos(t)ide agents. Here, TAF/TDF are tenofovir formulations, FTC is emtricitabine, and 3TC is lamivudine. Renal dysfunction, pregnancy, resistance, and interacting drugs can change the choice. [8] Common adult ART strategies Regimen or setting Practical use Reason to choose differently Bictegravir/FTC/TAF 50/200/25 mg PO daily One tablet daily; common rapid-start option Review kidney function and cations. Rifampin is contraindicated. Prior CAB PrEP requires a resistance-informed approach. [9] Dolutegravir 50 mg PO daily plus TAF/FTC or TDF/FTC Common initial alternative; select and dose the backbone for kidney function DTG dosing changes with some inducers or resistance. Fixed-dose combinations are not interchangeable across renal categories. [8] [10] Dolutegravir/3TC 50/300 mg PO daily Two-drug option for selected patients Do not use for rapid start before HBV/genotype results, with HBV coinfection, or HIV RNA >500,000 copies/mL. [8] [11] HIV after CAB PrEP Obtain integrase genotype; start boosted darunavir plus two appropriate NRTIs while results are pending Do not assume bictegravir or dolutegravir remains active. Pregnancy changes booster selection. [1] HIV/HBV coinfection Use TAF or TDF plus FTC or 3TC within suppressive ART FTC or 3TC alone is inadequate HBV treatment. If tenofovir cannot be used, add entecavir to fully suppressive HIV therapy. Avoid unplanned withdrawal of HBV-active drugs. [12] Pregnancy or pregnancy planning Start promptly and consult the current perinatal recommendations Do not withhold ART. Review pregnancy-specific pharmacokinetics and the complete regimen. [13] Fellow and attending discussion ART trial endpoints usually measure virologic suppression, not superiority in mortality. A switch study in already suppressed patients does not establish a rapid-start regimen. Distinguish the genetic barrier of a drug from the actual activity of the complete regimen against a patient’s archived virus. [8] [14]

Choose an effective complete regimen and account for the exceptions HIV integrates into host DNA and persists in a reservoir that current ART does not eradicate. NRTIs and NNRTIs inhibit reverse transcription, INSTIs inhibit integration, and protease inhibitors prevent viral maturation. Ritonavir and cobicistat commonly serve as pharmacokinetic boosters; they are not interchangeable with an active drug in the regimen. Capsid and entry-directed agents have specialized roles. slides.title: Fellow and attending discussion
slides.section: Choose an effective complete regimen and account for the exceptions
paragraphs: ART trial endpoints usually measure virologic suppression, not superiority in mortality. A switch study in already suppressed patients does not establish a rapid-start regimen. Distinguish the genetic barrier of a drug from the actual activity of the complete regimen against a patient’s archived virus. [8] [14]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Choose an effective complete regimen and account for the exceptions HIV integrates into host DNA and persists in a reservoir that current ART does not eradicate. NRTIs and NNRTIs inhibit reverse transcription, INSTIs inhibit integration, and protease inhibitors prevent viral maturation. Ritonavir and cobicistat commonly serve as pharmacokinetic boosters; they are not interchangeable with an active drug in the regimen. Capsid and entry-directed agents have specialized roles. [8] For most treatment-naive adults without prior long-acting cabotegravir exposure, initial treatment uses bictegravir/TAF/FTC or dolutegravir plus two nucleos(t)ide agents. Here, TAF/TDF are tenofovir formulations, FTC is emtricitabine, and 3TC is lamivudine. Renal dysfunction, pregnancy, resistance, and interacting drugs can change the choice. [8] Common adult ART strategies Regimen or setting Practical use Reason to choose differently Bictegravir/FTC/TAF 50/200/25 mg PO daily One tablet daily; common rapid-start option Review kidney function and cations. Rifampin is contraindicated. Prior CAB PrEP requires a resistance-informed approach. [9] Dolutegravir 50 mg PO daily plus TAF/FTC or TDF/FTC Common initial alternative; select and dose the backbone for kidney function DTG dosing changes with some inducers or resistance. Fixed-dose combinations are not interchangeable across renal categories. [8] [10] Dolutegravir/3TC 50/300 mg PO daily Two-drug option for selected patients Do not use for rapid start before HBV/genotype results, with HBV coinfection, or HIV RNA >500,000 copies/mL. [8] [11] HIV after CAB PrEP Obtain integrase genotype; start boosted darunavir plus two appropriate NRTIs while results are pending Do not assume bictegravir or dolutegravir remains active. Pregnancy changes booster selection. [1] HIV/HBV coinfection Use TAF or TDF plus FTC or 3TC within suppressive ART FTC or 3TC alone is inadequate HBV treatment. If tenofovir cannot be used, add entecavir to fully suppressive HIV therapy. Avoid unplanned withdrawal of HBV-active drugs. [12] Pregnancy or pregnancy planning Start promptly and consult the current perinatal recommendations Do not withhold ART. Review pregnancy-specific pharmacokinetics and the complete regimen. [13] Fellow and attending discussion ART trial endpoints usually measure virologic suppression, not superiority in mortality. A switch study in already suppressed patients does not establish a rapid-start regimen. Distinguish the genetic barrier of a drug from the actual activity of the complete regimen against a patient’s archived virus. [8] [14]

slides.title: Reconcile interactions and absorption before calling a regimen ineffective
slides.section: Reconcile interactions and absorption before calling a regimen ineffective
rows: Integrase inhibitors with magnesium/aluminum antacids, iron, calcium, or enteral feeds
Check the exact drug and administration schedule. Cation separation and food rules differ by product; ask pharmacy to document a feasible schedule.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Reconcile interactions and absorption before calling a regimen ineffective High-yield medication problems Problem Practical response Integrase inhibitors with magnesium/aluminum antacids, iron, calcium, or enteral feeds Check the exact drug and administration schedule. Cation separation and food rules differ by product; ask pharmacy to document a feasible schedule. Rifamycins with ART Use the TB/ART interaction tables. Do not add rifampin to bictegravir, CAB/RPV, or a boosted PI regimen without redesigning treatment. Ritonavir/cobicistat with corticosteroids, anticoagulants, statins, antiarrhythmics, or azoles A medication-level interaction check is mandatory. Inhaled or injected steroids also count. Oral rilpivirine with acid suppression or insufficient food PPIs are contraindicated with oral RPV; check food and H2-blocker timing. This absorption issue does not apply to injected RPV. Rising creatinine after DTG/BIC or cobicistat A small early change may reflect inhibited creatinine secretion, but assess true AKI, urine findings, nephrotoxins, and the trend. NPO, dysphagia, feeding tube, or ICU admission Verify formulations and product-specific crushing/dissolving data. Avoid accidental partial ART or an unplanned long-acting treatment gap. [15] [9] [8] [3] Repeat HIV RNA about 4-8 weeks after initiation or a regimen change, then every 4-8 weeks until suppressed. Stable suppression generally permits monitoring every 3-4 months, sometimes every 6 months after sustained stability. Follow CD4 more closely when it determines OI prevention. [16] For confirmed rebound at or above 200 copies/mL, assess access, adherence, interactions, and resistance. Obtain genotype while the failing regimen is still being taken, or preferably within 4 weeks of stopping oral ART. Review all historical resistance. A single low detectable result is not automatically failure. Do not add one active drug to a failing regimen. [14]

slides.title: Reconcile interactions and absorption before calling a regimen ineffective
slides.section: Reconcile interactions and absorption before calling a regimen ineffective
rows: Ritonavir/cobicistat with corticosteroids, anticoagulants, statins, antiarrhythmics, or azoles
A medication-level interaction check is mandatory. Inhaled or injected steroids also count.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Reconcile interactions and absorption before calling a regimen ineffective High-yield medication problems Problem Practical response Integrase inhibitors with magnesium/aluminum antacids, iron, calcium, or enteral feeds Check the exact drug and administration schedule. Cation separation and food rules differ by product; ask pharmacy to document a feasible schedule. Rifamycins with ART Use the TB/ART interaction tables. Do not add rifampin to bictegravir, CAB/RPV, or a boosted PI regimen without redesigning treatment. Ritonavir/cobicistat with corticosteroids, anticoagulants, statins, antiarrhythmics, or azoles A medication-level interaction check is mandatory. Inhaled or injected steroids also count. Oral rilpivirine with acid suppression or insufficient food PPIs are contraindicated with oral RPV; check food and H2-blocker timing. This absorption issue does not apply to injected RPV. Rising creatinine after DTG/BIC or cobicistat A small early change may reflect inhibited creatinine secretion, but assess true AKI, urine findings, nephrotoxins, and the trend. NPO, dysphagia, feeding tube, or ICU admission Verify formulations and product-specific crushing/dissolving data. Avoid accidental partial ART or an unplanned long-acting treatment gap. [15] [9] [8] [3] Repeat HIV RNA about 4-8 weeks after initiation or a regimen change, then every 4-8 weeks until suppressed. Stable suppression generally permits monitoring every 3-4 months, sometimes every 6 months after sustained stability. Follow CD4 more closely when it determines OI prevention. [16] For confirmed rebound at or above 200 copies/mL, assess access, adherence, interactions, and resistance. Obtain genotype while the failing regimen is still being taken, or preferably within 4 weeks of stopping oral ART. Review all historical resistance. A single low detectable result is not automatically failure. Do not add one active drug to a failing regimen. [14]

slides.title: OI next steps start with the syndrome and severity
slides.section: OI next steps start with the syndrome and severity
paragraphs: Second teaching block · OI diagnosis and treatment
Doses below are adult starting examples, not individualized orders. Adjust for renal/hepatic function, weight, pregnancy, formulation, and drug interactions; confirm with pharmacy.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
OI next steps start with the syndrome and severity Second teaching block · OI diagnosis and treatment Doses below are adult starting examples, not individualized orders. Adjust for renal/hepatic function, weight, pregnancy, formulation, and drug interactions; confirm with pharmacy. CD4 thresholds change probability; they are not exclusion rules. Bacterial infections and TB can occur at any CD4 count. Below 200, PCP becomes prominent; below 100, consider toxoplasmosis and cryptococcosis; below 50, disseminated MAC and CMV end-organ disease become more likely. Histoplasmosis is particularly important with advanced HIV and relevant geography. [6] [5] [7] [17] [18] [19] [3] Syndrome-directed OI assessment Presentation Diagnostic next steps Immediate treatment or action Subacute dyspnea, dry cough, hypoxemia Pulse oximetry, imaging; arterial blood gas when steroid threshold is uncertain. Induced sputum or BAL for PCP testing; assess bacterial pneumonia and TB concurrently. Treat suspected severe PCP promptly while obtaining confirmation. Add oxygen and indicated corticosteroids; isolate for TB if suspected. Headache, meningitis, altered mentation Neurologic exam; imaging before LP when indicated. LP with opening pressure, cell count, glucose/protein, CrAg, and fungal culture; other tests guided by presentation. Treat the likely syndrome urgently; do not start ART reflexively before assessing cryptococcal/TB meningitis. Focal deficit or seizure Contrast MRI; Toxoplasma IgG; consider lymphoma, PML, TB, abscess, stroke. CSF only if safe. Treat presumed toxoplasmosis when supported; arrange early biopsy for atypical features or lack of response. Floaters, scotoma, blurred vision Urgent dilated retinal examination; do not use plasma CMV PCR to rule out retinitis. slides.section: OI next steps start with the syndrome and severity
rows: Contrast MRI; Toxoplasma IgG; consider lymphoma, PML, TB, abscess, stroke. CSF only if safe.
Treat presumed toxoplasmosis when supported; arrange early biopsy for atypical features or lack of response.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
OI next steps start with the syndrome and severity Second teaching block · OI diagnosis and treatment Doses below are adult starting examples, not individualized orders. Adjust for renal/hepatic function, weight, pregnancy, formulation, and drug interactions; confirm with pharmacy. CD4 thresholds change probability; they are not exclusion rules. Bacterial infections and TB can occur at any CD4 count. Below 200, PCP becomes prominent; below 100, consider toxoplasmosis and cryptococcosis; below 50, disseminated MAC and CMV end-organ disease become more likely. Histoplasmosis is particularly important with advanced HIV and relevant geography. [6] [5] [7] [17] [18] [19] [3] Syndrome-directed OI assessment Presentation Diagnostic next steps Immediate treatment or action Subacute dyspnea, dry cough, hypoxemia Pulse oximetry, imaging; arterial blood gas when steroid threshold is uncertain. Induced sputum or BAL for PCP testing; assess bacterial pneumonia and TB concurrently. Treat suspected severe PCP promptly while obtaining confirmation. Add oxygen and indicated corticosteroids; isolate for TB if suspected. Headache, meningitis, altered mentation Neurologic exam; imaging before LP when indicated. LP with opening pressure, cell count, glucose/protein, CrAg, and fungal culture; other tests guided by presentation. Treat the likely syndrome urgently; do not start ART reflexively before assessing cryptococcal/TB meningitis. Focal deficit or seizure Contrast MRI; Toxoplasma IgG; consider lymphoma, PML, TB, abscess, stroke. CSF only if safe. Treat presumed toxoplasmosis when supported; arrange early biopsy for atypical features or lack of response. Floaters, scotoma, blurred vision Urgent dilated retinal examination; do not use plasma CMV PCR to rule out retinitis. Same-day ophthalmology; sight-threatening disease may need local plus systemic therapy. Fever, wasting, cytopenias, high alkaline phosphatase Blood cultures; mycobacterial blood cultures, urine/serum Histoplasma antigen, imaging and tissue sampling as indicated. Consider lymphoma. In severe disseminated histoplasmosis, begin liposomal amphotericin B. Avoid macrolide prophylaxis while evaluating possible active MAC. Odynophagia or persistent diarrhea Assess thrush, stool tests and exact panel coverage, medications, hydration. Endoscopy with biopsy when esophageal disease fails empiric treatment or CMV colitis is suspected. Systemic antifungal for esophageal candidiasis; rehydration and organism-directed enteric therapy. CMV DNAemia alone does not establish colitis. [6] [7] [5] [20] [18] [19] [17] [21] [22] Source control still matters. Drain an ordinary bacterial abscess, remove infected hardware when indicated, and obtain tissue when it will distinguish infection from malignancy. In cryptococcal meningitis, pressure management with therapeutic LP is essential alongside antifungal therapy.

slides.title: OI next steps start with the syndrome and severity
slides.section: OI next steps start with the syndrome and severity
rows: Assess thrush, stool tests and exact panel coverage, medications, hydration. Endoscopy with biopsy when esophageal disease fails empiric treatment or CMV colitis is suspected.
Systemic antifungal for esophageal candidiasis; rehydration and organism-directed enteric therapy. CMV DNAemia alone does not establish colitis.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
OI next steps start with the syndrome and severity Second teaching block · OI diagnosis and treatment Doses below are adult starting examples, not individualized orders. Adjust for renal/hepatic function, weight, pregnancy, formulation, and drug interactions; confirm with pharmacy. CD4 thresholds change probability; they are not exclusion rules. Bacterial infections and TB can occur at any CD4 count. Below 200, PCP becomes prominent; below 100, consider toxoplasmosis and cryptococcosis; below 50, disseminated MAC and CMV end-organ disease become more likely. Histoplasmosis is particularly important with advanced HIV and relevant geography. [6] [5] [7] [17] [18] [19] [3] Syndrome-directed OI assessment Presentation Diagnostic next steps Immediate treatment or action Subacute dyspnea, dry cough, hypoxemia Pulse oximetry, imaging; arterial blood gas when steroid threshold is uncertain. Induced sputum or BAL for PCP testing; assess bacterial pneumonia and TB concurrently. Treat suspected severe PCP promptly while obtaining confirmation. Add oxygen and indicated corticosteroids; isolate for TB if suspected. Headache, meningitis, altered mentation Neurologic exam; imaging before LP when indicated. LP with opening pressure, cell count, glucose/protein, CrAg, and fungal culture; other tests guided by presentation. Treat the likely syndrome urgently; do not start ART reflexively before assessing cryptococcal/TB meningitis. Focal deficit or seizure Contrast MRI; Toxoplasma IgG; consider lymphoma, PML, TB, abscess, stroke. CSF only if safe. Treat presumed toxoplasmosis when supported; arrange early biopsy for atypical features or lack of response. Floaters, scotoma, blurred vision Urgent dilated retinal examination; do not use plasma CMV PCR to rule out retinitis. Same-day ophthalmology; sight-threatening disease may need local plus systemic therapy. Fever, wasting, cytopenias, high alkaline phosphatase Blood cultures; mycobacterial blood cultures, urine/serum Histoplasma antigen, imaging and tissue sampling as indicated. Consider lymphoma. In severe disseminated histoplasmosis, begin liposomal amphotericin B. Avoid macrolide prophylaxis while evaluating possible active MAC. Odynophagia or persistent diarrhea Assess thrush, stool tests and exact panel coverage, medications, hydration. Endoscopy with biopsy when esophageal disease fails empiric treatment or CMV colitis is suspected. Systemic antifungal for esophageal candidiasis; rehydration and organism-directed enteric therapy. CMV DNAemia alone does not establish colitis. [6] [7] [5] [20] [18] [19] [17] [21] [22] Source control still matters. Drain an ordinary bacterial abscess, remove infected hardware when indicated, and obtain tissue when it will distinguish infection from malignancy. In cryptococcal meningitis, pressure management with therapeutic LP is essential alongside antifungal therapy.

slides.title: PCP treatment depends on respiratory severity and is followed by secondary prophylaxis
slides.section: PCP treatment depends on respiratory severity and is followed by secondary prophylaxis
paragraphs: Confirm with respiratory staining or PCR on an appropriate specimen. PCR may detect colonization; beta-D-glucan supports but does not establish the diagnosis. A normal chest radiograph does not exclude PCP. Consider coinfection. [6]

Treat for 21 days with TMP-SMX, dosed by TMP at 15-20 mg/kg/day, divided every 6-8 hours IV for moderate/severe disease; oral therapy is appropriate for mild disease or after improvement. Adjust for renal function. Monitor potassium, creatinine, CBC, liver tests, and rash. [6]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
PCP treatment depends on respiratory severity and is followed by secondary prophylaxis Confirm with respiratory staining or PCR on an appropriate specimen. PCR may detect colonization; beta-D-glucan supports but does not establish the diagnosis. A normal chest radiograph does not exclude PCP. Consider coinfection. [6] Treat for 21 days with TMP-SMX, dosed by TMP at 15-20 mg/kg/day, divided every 6-8 hours IV for moderate/severe disease; oral therapy is appropriate for mild disease or after improvement. Adjust for renal function. Monitor potassium, creatinine, CBC, liver tests, and rash. [6] Add prednisone if room-air PaO₂ is <70 mmHg or the A-a gradient is ≥35 mmHg. Start ideally within 72 hours: 40 mg twice daily on days 1-5, 40 mg daily on days 6-10, then 20 mg daily on days 11-21. [6] Alternatives include clindamycin-primaquine or IV pentamidine for moderate/severe disease, and atovaquone for mild disease. Check G6PD before primaquine or dapsone. Start ART within 2 weeks when feasible; begin secondary prophylaxis immediately after treatment. [6] Before escalating for apparent failure, reassess oxygenation, absorption, toxicity, fluid status, pneumothorax, and another infection. Clinical worsening is not itself proof of resistance.

slides.title: PCP treatment depends on respiratory severity and is followed by secondary prophylaxis
slides.section: PCP treatment depends on respiratory severity and is followed by secondary prophylaxis
paragraphs: Add prednisone if room-air PaO₂ is <70 mmHg or the A-a gradient is ≥35 mmHg. Start ideally within 72 hours: 40 mg twice daily on days 1-5, 40 mg daily on days 6-10, then 20 mg daily on days 11-21. [6]

Alternatives include clindamycin-primaquine or IV pentamidine for moderate/severe disease, and atovaquone for mild disease. Check G6PD before primaquine or dapsone. Start ART within 2 weeks when feasible; begin secondary prophylaxis immediately after treatment. [6]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
PCP treatment depends on respiratory severity and is followed by secondary prophylaxis Confirm with respiratory staining or PCR on an appropriate specimen. PCR may detect colonization; beta-D-glucan supports but does not establish the diagnosis. A normal chest radiograph does not exclude PCP. Consider coinfection. [6] Treat for 21 days with TMP-SMX, dosed by TMP at 15-20 mg/kg/day, divided every 6-8 hours IV for moderate/severe disease; oral therapy is appropriate for mild disease or after improvement. Adjust for renal function. Monitor potassium, creatinine, CBC, liver tests, and rash. [6] Add prednisone if room-air PaO₂ is <70 mmHg or the A-a gradient is ≥35 mmHg. Start ideally within 72 hours: 40 mg twice daily on days 1-5, 40 mg daily on days 6-10, then 20 mg daily on days 11-21. [6] Alternatives include clindamycin-primaquine or IV pentamidine for moderate/severe disease, and atovaquone for mild disease. Check G6PD before primaquine or dapsone. Start ART within 2 weeks when feasible; begin secondary prophylaxis immediately after treatment. [6] Before escalating for apparent failure, reassess oxygenation, absorption, toxicity, fluid status, pneumothorax, and another infection. Clinical worsening is not itself proof of resistance.

slides.title: Cryptococcal meningitis requires antifungal treatment and active pressure management
slides.section: Cryptococcal meningitis requires antifungal treatment and active pressure management
paragraphs: Send serum and CSF CrAg and CSF fungal culture; measure opening pressure. A negative meningitis-panel PCR does not exclude cryptococcosis. Symptomatic elevated pressure requires therapeutic LPs, often repeated daily. Do not use serial CrAg titers to document clearance. [7]

U.S. preferred induction is liposomal amphotericin B 3-4 mg/kg IV daily plus flucytosine 25 mg/kg PO every 6 hours for 2 weeks, with renal adjustment and drug-level monitoring for flucytosine. Follow CBC, renal function, potassium, and magnesium. Reassess CSF culture at about days 7 and 14. [7]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Cryptococcal meningitis requires antifungal treatment and active pressure management Send serum and CSF CrAg and CSF fungal culture; measure opening pressure. A negative meningitis-panel PCR does not exclude cryptococcosis. Symptomatic elevated pressure requires therapeutic LPs, often repeated daily. Do not use serial CrAg titers to document clearance. [7] U.S. preferred induction is liposomal amphotericin B 3-4 mg/kg IV daily plus flucytosine 25 mg/kg PO every 6 hours for 2 weeks, with renal adjustment and drug-level monitoring for flucytosine. Follow CBC, renal function, potassium, and magnesium. Reassess CSF culture at about days 7 and 14. [7] Consolidate with fluconazole 800 mg daily for at least 8 weeks; once stable with sterile CSF and ART initiated, 400 mg daily may be used. Then fluconazole 200 mg daily for maintenance. If CSF remains culture-positive after induction, adjust the induction/consolidation plan and continue consolidation for at least 8 weeks from documented CSF culture clearance. Instability also requires reassessment. [7] Defer ART approximately 4-6 weeks after antifungal initiation. Stop maintenance only after ≥1 year of antifungals, absent symptoms, CD4 ≥100, and suppressed HIV RNA. Avoid routine steroids, acetazolamide, or mannitol for cryptococcal pressure management. [7] Fellow and attending discussion The single-dose liposomal amphotericin strategy studied in African settings includes 14 days of flucytosine and high-dose fluconazole. It is not one-dose monotherapy. The care setting and monitoring requirements matter. [7]

slides.title: Cryptococcal meningitis requires antifungal treatment and active pressure management
slides.section: Cryptococcal meningitis requires antifungal treatment and active pressure management
paragraphs: Consolidate with fluconazole 800 mg daily for at least 8 weeks; once stable with sterile CSF and ART initiated, 400 mg daily may be used. Then fluconazole 200 mg daily for maintenance. If CSF remains culture-positive after induction, adjust the induction/consolidation plan and continue consolidation for at least 8 weeks from documented CSF culture clearance. Instability also requires reassessment. [7]

Defer ART approximately 4-6 weeks after antifungal initiation. Stop maintenance only after ≥1 year of antifungals, absent symptoms, CD4 ≥100, and suppressed HIV RNA. Avoid routine steroids, acetazolamide, or mannitol for cryptococcal pressure management. [7]

Complete source section:

A negative meningitis-panel PCR does not exclude cryptococcosis. Symptomatic elevated pressure requires therapeutic LPs, often repeated daily. Do not use serial CrAg titers to document clearance. [7] U.S. preferred induction is liposomal amphotericin B 3-4 mg/kg IV daily plus flucytosine 25 mg/kg PO every 6 hours for 2 weeks, with renal adjustment and drug-level monitoring for flucytosine. Follow CBC, renal function, potassium, and magnesium. Reassess CSF culture at about days 7 and 14. slides.title: Treat likely toxoplasma encephalitis while preserving a path to another diagnosis
slides.section: Treat likely toxoplasma encephalitis while preserving a path to another diagnosis
paragraphs: In advanced HIV, multiple enhancing lesions plus positive Toxoplasma IgG support a presumptive diagnosis. MRI is more sensitive than CT. Negative IgG or CSF PCR does not absolutely exclude disease. Consider lymphoma, TB, bacterial abscess, and fungal infection. [5]

Preferred acute therapy is TMP-SMX at TMP 5 mg/kg plus SMX 25 mg/kg IV or PO twice daily, or pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine-leucovorin. For the latter, give pyrimethamine 200 mg once, then 50 mg daily if ≤60 kg or 75 mg daily if >60 kg; sulfadiazine 1 g or 1.5 g every 6 hours respectively; leucovorin 10-25 mg daily. Treat ≥6 weeks, longer for extensive or incompletely resolved disease. [5]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Treat likely toxoplasma encephalitis while preserving a path to another diagnosis In advanced HIV, multiple enhancing lesions plus positive Toxoplasma IgG support a presumptive diagnosis. MRI is more sensitive than CT. Negative IgG or CSF PCR does not absolutely exclude disease. Consider lymphoma, TB, bacterial abscess, and fungal infection. [5] Preferred acute therapy is TMP-SMX at TMP 5 mg/kg plus SMX 25 mg/kg IV or PO twice daily, or pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine-leucovorin. For the latter, give pyrimethamine 200 mg once, then 50 mg daily if ≤60 kg or 75 mg daily if >60 kg; sulfadiazine 1 g or 1.5 g every 6 hours respectively; leucovorin 10-25 mg daily. Treat ≥6 weeks, longer for extensive or incompletely resolved disease. [5] Reconsider the diagnosis and biopsy if deteriorating early or not improving by 10-14 days. Use steroids only for clinically important edema/mass effect; lymphoma can also improve with steroids. Treat seizures if present. [5] ART often begins around 2-3 weeks; evidence for an exact interval is limited. Maintenance options include TMP-SMX DS twice daily. Stop after completed acute therapy, no symptoms, and CD4 >200 for >6 months on ART. [5]

slides.title: Diagnose CMV end-organ disease in the organ involved
slides.section: Diagnose CMV end-organ disease in the organ involved
paragraphs: Retinitis requires expert retinal examination. Plasma CMV PCR neither confirms nor excludes it. GI disease generally requires compatible endoscopy and tissue evidence; shedding or DNAemia alone is insufficient. Arrange baseline ophthalmology when CD4 <100 and urgent assessment for new visual symptoms. [18]

Retinitis induction uses valganciclovir 900 mg PO twice daily or ganciclovir 5 mg/kg IV every 12 hours for 14-21 days, guided by retinal response. Sight-threatening lesions may also require intravitreal therapy. Maintenance is usually valganciclovir 900 mg daily. Adjust for renal function and monitor CBC and creatinine. [18]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Diagnose CMV end-organ disease in the organ involved Retinitis requires expert retinal examination. Plasma CMV PCR neither confirms nor excludes it. GI disease generally requires compatible endoscopy and tissue evidence; shedding or DNAemia alone is insufficient. Arrange baseline ophthalmology when CD4 <100 and urgent assessment for new visual symptoms. [18] Retinitis induction uses valganciclovir 900 mg PO twice daily or ganciclovir 5 mg/kg IV every 12 hours for 14-21 days, guided by retinal response. Sight-threatening lesions may also require intravitreal therapy. Maintenance is usually valganciclovir 900 mg daily. Adjust for renal function and monitor CBC and creatinine. [18] For colitis/esophagitis, IV ganciclovir may transition to oral valganciclovir when absorption is adequate; treat 21-42 days until clinical resolution. Maintenance is usually unnecessary after resolved GI disease unless concurrent retinitis, recurrence, or severe initial disease. Start ART within 1-2 weeks for most CMV end-organ disease. [18] Retinitis maintenance can stop with ophthalmology after ≥3 months of therapy, inactive lesions, and CD4 ≥100 for ≥3 months on ART. Do not prescribe valganciclovir primary prophylaxis solely for low CD4 or positive blood PCR. [18]

slides.title: Disseminated MAC
slides.section: Distinguish disseminated MAC, histoplasmosis, and TB before choosing long treatment
paragraphs: Obtain mycobacterial blood culture or involved-tissue culture and macrolide susceptibility. A respiratory isolate alone does not establish disseminated disease. Use clarithromycin 500 mg PO twice daily plus ethambutol 15 mg/kg daily; azithromycin 500-600 mg daily is an alternative when interactions, intolerance, or adherence preclude clarithromycin. Consider rifabutin as a third agent in severe/high-burden disease or without viral suppression, adjusting for ART interactions. Start ART promptly, preferably with MAC treatment. [17]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Distinguish disseminated MAC, histoplasmosis, and TB before choosing long treatment Disseminated MAC Obtain mycobacterial blood culture or involved-tissue culture and macrolide susceptibility. A respiratory isolate alone does not establish disseminated disease. Use clarithromycin 500 mg PO twice daily plus ethambutol 15 mg/kg daily; azithromycin 500-600 mg daily is an alternative when interactions, intolerance, or adherence preclude clarithromycin. Consider rifabutin as a third agent in severe/high-burden disease or without viral suppression, adjusting for ART interactions. Start ART promptly, preferably with MAC treatment. [17] Treat ≥12 months and until asymptomatic with CD4 >100 for ≥6 months on ART. Follow vision/color discrimination with ethambutol, liver tests, QT/interactions, and clinical response. Persistent symptoms require reassessment of cultures, resistance, another infection, lymphoma, or IRIS. [17] Disseminated histoplasmosis Consider with fever, weight loss, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, or elevated alkaline phosphatase, especially in the Mississippi/Ohio River valleys. Send urine/serum antigen and obtain fungal cultures or tissue when indicated; antigen cross-reactivity can limit specificity. [19] Severe disease: liposomal amphotericin B 3 mg/kg IV daily for ≥2 weeks or until improved, then itraconazole 200 mg PO three times daily for 3 days followed by twice daily for ≥12 months. Mild/moderate disease can start itraconazole. Check formulation, interactions, levels after about 2 weeks, liver tests, and serial antigen. CNS disease requires a different, longer amphotericin induction. Start ART promptly after antifungals. [19] Tuberculosis Use airborne precautions for suspected pulmonary/laryngeal TB; obtain respiratory AFB smear, culture, NAAT and resistance testing. A negative IGRA does not exclude disease. Standard susceptible-TB therapy uses isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol initially, then isoniazid/rifampin when eligibility is established. Rifamycin-ART interactions must be resolved before prescribing. [3] Without meningitis, start ART within 2 weeks if CD4 <50 and within 2-8 weeks if ≥50. TB meningitis needs a separate decision: NIH permits ART after ≥2 weeks once controlled, while ATS/CDC/IDSA guidance has favored waiting 8 weeks. Document the rationale with the TB team. [3] Open the TB module for doses, duration exceptions, latent infection, resistant TB, and newer regimens.

slides.title: Disseminated MAC
slides.section: Distinguish disseminated MAC, histoplasmosis, and TB before choosing long treatment
paragraphs: Treat ≥12 months and until asymptomatic with CD4 >100 for ≥6 months on ART. Follow vision/color discrimination with ethambutol, liver tests, QT/interactions, and clinical response. Persistent symptoms require reassessment of cultures, resistance, another infection, lymphoma, or IRIS. [17]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Distinguish disseminated MAC, histoplasmosis, and TB before choosing long treatment Disseminated MAC Obtain mycobacterial blood culture or involved-tissue culture and macrolide susceptibility. A respiratory isolate alone does not establish disseminated disease. Use clarithromycin 500 mg PO twice daily plus ethambutol 15 mg/kg daily; azithromycin 500-600 mg daily is an alternative when interactions, intolerance, or adherence preclude clarithromycin. Consider rifabutin as a third agent in severe/high-burden disease or without viral suppression, adjusting for ART interactions. Start ART promptly, preferably with MAC treatment. [17] Treat ≥12 months and until asymptomatic with CD4 >100 for ≥6 months on ART. Follow vision/color discrimination with ethambutol, liver tests, QT/interactions, and clinical response. Persistent symptoms require reassessment of cultures, resistance, another infection, lymphoma, or IRIS. [17] Disseminated histoplasmosis Consider with fever, weight loss, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, or elevated alkaline phosphatase, especially in the Mississippi/Ohio River valleys. Send urine/serum antigen and obtain fungal cultures or tissue when indicated; antigen cross-reactivity can limit specificity. [19] Severe disease: liposomal amphotericin B 3 mg/kg IV daily for ≥2 weeks or until improved, then itraconazole 200 mg PO three times daily for 3 days followed by twice daily for ≥12 months. Mild/moderate disease can start itraconazole. Check formulation, interactions, levels after about 2 weeks, liver tests, and serial antigen. CNS disease requires a different, longer amphotericin induction. Start ART promptly after antifungals. [19] Tuberculosis Use airborne precautions for suspected pulmonary/laryngeal TB; obtain respiratory AFB smear, culture, NAAT and resistance testing. A negative IGRA does not exclude disease. Standard susceptible-TB therapy uses isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol initially, then isoniazid/rifampin when eligibility is established. Rifamycin-ART interactions must be resolved before prescribing. [3] Without meningitis, start ART within 2 weeks if CD4 <50 and within 2-8 weeks if ≥50. TB meningitis needs a separate decision: NIH permits ART after ≥2 weeks once controlled, while ATS/CDC/IDSA guidance has favored waiting 8 weeks. Document the rationale with the TB team. [3] Open the TB module for doses, duration exceptions, latent infection, resistant TB, and newer regimens.

slides.title: Tuberculosis
slides.section: Distinguish disseminated MAC, histoplasmosis, and TB before choosing long treatment
paragraphs: Use airborne precautions for suspected pulmonary/laryngeal TB; obtain respiratory AFB smear, culture, NAAT and resistance testing. A negative IGRA does not exclude disease. Standard susceptible-TB therapy uses isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol initially, then isoniazid/rifampin when eligibility is established. Rifamycin-ART interactions must be resolved before prescribing. [3]

Without meningitis, start ART within 2 weeks if CD4 <50 and within 2-8 weeks if ≥50. TB meningitis needs a separate decision: NIH permits ART after ≥2 weeks once controlled, while ATS/CDC/IDSA guidance has favored waiting 8 weeks. Document the rationale with the TB team. [3]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Distinguish disseminated MAC, histoplasmosis, and TB before choosing long treatment Disseminated MAC Obtain mycobacterial blood culture or involved-tissue culture and macrolide susceptibility. A respiratory isolate alone does not establish disseminated disease. Use clarithromycin 500 mg PO twice daily plus ethambutol 15 mg/kg daily; azithromycin 500-600 mg daily is an alternative when interactions, intolerance, or adherence preclude clarithromycin. Consider rifabutin as a third agent in severe/high-burden disease or without viral suppression, adjusting for ART interactions. Start ART promptly, preferably with MAC treatment. [17] Treat ≥12 months and until asymptomatic with CD4 >100 for ≥6 months on ART. Follow vision/color discrimination with ethambutol, liver tests, QT/interactions, and clinical response. Persistent symptoms require reassessment of cultures, resistance, another infection, lymphoma, or IRIS. [17] Disseminated histoplasmosis Consider with fever, weight loss, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, or elevated alkaline phosphatase, especially in the Mississippi/Ohio River valleys. Send urine/serum antigen and obtain fungal cultures or tissue when indicated; antigen cross-reactivity can limit specificity. [19] Severe disease: liposomal amphotericin B 3 mg/kg IV daily for ≥2 weeks or until improved, then itraconazole 200 mg PO three times daily for 3 days followed by twice daily for ≥12 months. Mild/moderate disease can start itraconazole. Check formulation, interactions, levels after about 2 weeks, liver tests, and serial antigen. CNS disease requires a different, longer amphotericin induction. Start ART promptly after antifungals. [19] Tuberculosis Use airborne precautions for suspected pulmonary/laryngeal TB; obtain respiratory AFB smear, culture, NAAT and resistance testing. A negative IGRA does not exclude disease. Standard susceptible-TB therapy uses isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol initially, then isoniazid/rifampin when eligibility is established. Rifamycin-ART interactions must be resolved before prescribing. [3] Without meningitis, start ART within 2 weeks if CD4 <50 and within 2-8 weeks if ≥50. TB meningitis needs a separate decision: NIH permits ART after ≥2 weeks once controlled, while ATS/CDC/IDSA guidance has favored waiting 8 weeks. Document the rationale with the TB team. [3] Open the TB module for doses, duration exceptions, latent infection, resistant TB, and newer regimens.

slides.title: Mucosal, enteric, neurologic, and related infections need distinct diagnostic pathways
slides.section: Mucosal, enteric, neurologic, and related infections need distinct diagnostic pathways
rows: Systemic fluconazole, 200 mg loading then 100-200 mg daily (up to 400 mg), for 14-21 days. Oral suspension can help swallowing.
No improvement within about 7 days warrants endoscopy, culture/speciation, and biopsy for CMV/HSV or another cause. Topical therapy is inadequate. [21]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Mucosal, enteric, neurologic, and related infections need distinct diagnostic pathways Additional OIs and related infections Syndrome Diagnosis and treatment Decision that changes management Esophageal candidiasis Systemic fluconazole, 200 mg loading then 100-200 mg daily (up to 400 mg), for 14-21 days. Oral suspension can help swallowing. No improvement within about 7 days warrants endoscopy, culture/speciation, and biopsy for CMV/HSV or another cause. Topical therapy is inadequate. [21] Cryptosporidiosis Stool antigen, PCR, or appropriate stain; rehydration, electrolyte replacement, and effective ART are central. Nitazoxanide 500-1,000 mg twice daily with food for ≥14 days may be considered. Drug evidence in advanced HIV is limited. Do not substitute antiparasitic therapy for immune restoration. [22] Cystoisosporiasis Request appropriate stool testing; routine multiplex panels may omit it. TMP-SMX DS twice daily for 7 days or four times daily for 10 days. Persistent disease may need longer/higher-dose treatment; maintenance TMP-SMX is used with CD4 <200. [23] Microsporidiosis Special stool studies or tissue testing; ART and supportive care. Treatment depends on species. Albendazole is active for several species but is unreliable for Enterocytozoon bieneusi; confirm species and specialist access options. [24] PML Progressive focal deficits, characteristic white-matter MRI lesions, and CSF JCV PCR. Repeat testing or biopsy if suspicion remains despite negative PCR. Initiate effective ART immediately. No established JCV-directed antiviral treatment; edema-producing PML-IRIS may require steroids. [20] Severe HSV or disseminated VZV Lesion PCR and organ-directed testing. Severe HSV often requires IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours; extensive/disseminated VZV also requires IV therapy. Adjust for renal function, hydrate, assess CNS/ocular involvement. Nonhealing HSV despite therapy raises resistance; obtain culture/susceptibility and expert treatment. [25] [26] Bacterial pneumonia or sepsis Standard syndrome-based cultures, imaging, resuscitation, and antibiotics. Broaden for documented resistant-organism risk or severe disease. HIV alone does not justify indefinite MRSA or antipseudomonal therapy. Consider simultaneous PCP/TB and obtain source control when needed. [27] Syphilis, including ocular or neurologic disease Interpret treponemal/nontreponemal tests with prior treatment and symptoms. Stage-appropriate therapy generally matches treatment without HIV. Ocular, otic, or neurologic disease changes evaluation and treatment. Neurosyphilis uses aqueous penicillin G 18-24 million units/day IV for 10-14 days; benzathine penicillin alone is inadequate. [28] Kaposi sarcoma, lymphoma, medication toxicity, inflammatory disease, and ordinary community infections belong in the differential. A positive low-specificity test should not prevent tissue diagnosis when the clinical picture is inconsistent.

slides.title: Mucosal, enteric, neurologic, and related infections need distinct diagnostic pathways
slides.section: Mucosal, enteric, neurologic, and related infections need distinct diagnostic pathways
rows: Stool antigen, PCR, or appropriate stain; rehydration, electrolyte replacement, and effective ART are central. Nitazoxanide 500-1,000 mg twice daily with food for ≥14 days may be considered.
Drug evidence in advanced HIV is limited. Do not substitute antiparasitic therapy for immune restoration. [22]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Mucosal, enteric, neurologic, and related infections need distinct diagnostic pathways Additional OIs and related infections Syndrome Diagnosis and treatment Decision that changes management Esophageal candidiasis Systemic fluconazole, 200 mg loading then 100-200 mg daily (up to 400 mg), for 14-21 days. Oral suspension can help swallowing. No improvement within about 7 days warrants endoscopy, culture/speciation, and biopsy for CMV/HSV or another cause. Topical therapy is inadequate. [21] Cryptosporidiosis Stool antigen, PCR, or appropriate stain; rehydration, electrolyte replacement, and effective ART are central. Nitazoxanide 500-1,000 mg twice daily with food for ≥14 days may be considered. Drug evidence in advanced HIV is limited. Do not substitute antiparasitic therapy for immune restoration. [22] Cystoisosporiasis Request appropriate stool testing; routine multiplex panels may omit it. TMP-SMX DS twice daily for 7 days or four times daily for 10 days. Persistent disease may need longer/higher-dose treatment; maintenance TMP-SMX is used with CD4 <200. [23] Microsporidiosis Special stool studies or tissue testing; ART and supportive care. Treatment depends on species. Albendazole is active for several species but is unreliable for Enterocytozoon bieneusi; confirm species and specialist access options. [24] PML Progressive focal deficits, characteristic white-matter MRI lesions, and CSF JCV PCR. Repeat testing or biopsy if suspicion remains despite negative PCR. Initiate effective ART immediately. No established JCV-directed antiviral treatment; edema-producing PML-IRIS may require steroids. [20] Severe HSV or disseminated VZV Lesion PCR and organ-directed testing. Severe HSV often requires IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours; extensive/disseminated VZV also requires IV therapy. Adjust for renal function, hydrate, assess CNS/ocular involvement. Nonhealing HSV despite therapy raises resistance; obtain culture/susceptibility and expert treatment. [25] [26] Bacterial pneumonia or sepsis Standard syndrome-based cultures, imaging, resuscitation, and antibiotics. Broaden for documented resistant-organism risk or severe disease. HIV alone does not justify indefinite MRSA or antipseudomonal therapy. Consider simultaneous PCP/TB and obtain source control when needed. [27] Syphilis, including ocular or neurologic disease Interpret treponemal/nontreponemal tests with prior treatment and symptoms. Stage-appropriate therapy generally matches treatment without HIV. Ocular, otic, or neurologic disease changes evaluation and treatment. Neurosyphilis uses aqueous penicillin G 18-24 million units/day IV for 10-14 days; benzathine penicillin alone is inadequate. [28] Kaposi sarcoma, lymphoma, medication toxicity, inflammatory disease, and ordinary community infections belong in the differential. A positive low-specificity test should not prevent tissue diagnosis when the clinical picture is inconsistent.

slides.title: Mucosal, enteric, neurologic, and related infections need distinct diagnostic pathways
slides.section: Mucosal, enteric, neurologic, and related infections need distinct diagnostic pathways
rows: Progressive focal deficits, characteristic white-matter MRI lesions, and CSF JCV PCR. Repeat testing or biopsy if suspicion remains despite negative PCR.
Initiate effective ART immediately. No established JCV-directed antiviral treatment; edema-producing PML-IRIS may require steroids. [20]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Mucosal, enteric, neurologic, and related infections need distinct diagnostic pathways Additional OIs and related infections Syndrome Diagnosis and treatment Decision that changes management Esophageal candidiasis Systemic fluconazole, 200 mg loading then 100-200 mg daily (up to 400 mg), for 14-21 days. Oral suspension can help swallowing. No improvement within about 7 days warrants endoscopy, culture/speciation, and biopsy for CMV/HSV or another cause. Topical therapy is inadequate. [21] Cryptosporidiosis Stool antigen, PCR, or appropriate stain; rehydration, electrolyte replacement, and effective ART are central. Nitazoxanide 500-1,000 mg twice daily with food for ≥14 days may be considered. Drug evidence in advanced HIV is limited. Do not substitute antiparasitic therapy for immune restoration. [22] Cystoisosporiasis Request appropriate stool testing; routine multiplex panels may omit it. TMP-SMX DS twice daily for 7 days or four times daily for 10 days. Persistent disease may need longer/higher-dose treatment; maintenance TMP-SMX is used with CD4 <200. [23] Microsporidiosis Special stool studies or tissue testing; ART and supportive care. Treatment depends on species. Albendazole is active for several species but is unreliable for Enterocytozoon bieneusi; confirm species and specialist access options. [24] PML Progressive focal deficits, characteristic white-matter MRI lesions, and CSF JCV PCR. Repeat testing or biopsy if suspicion remains despite negative PCR. Initiate effective ART immediately. No established JCV-directed antiviral treatment; edema-producing PML-IRIS may require steroids. [20] Severe HSV or disseminated VZV Lesion PCR and organ-directed testing. Severe HSV often requires IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours; extensive/disseminated VZV also requires IV therapy. Adjust for renal function, hydrate, assess CNS/ocular involvement. Nonhealing HSV despite therapy raises resistance; obtain culture/susceptibility and expert treatment. [25] [26] Bacterial pneumonia or sepsis Standard syndrome-based cultures, imaging, resuscitation, and antibiotics. Broaden for documented resistant-organism risk or severe disease. HIV alone does not justify indefinite MRSA or antipseudomonal therapy. Consider simultaneous PCP/TB and obtain source control when needed. [27] Syphilis, including ocular or neurologic disease Interpret treponemal/nontreponemal tests with prior treatment and symptoms. Stage-appropriate therapy generally matches treatment without HIV. Ocular, otic, or neurologic disease changes evaluation and treatment. Neurosyphilis uses aqueous penicillin G 18-24 million units/day IV for 10-14 days; benzathine penicillin alone is inadequate. [28] Kaposi sarcoma, lymphoma, medication toxicity, inflammatory disease, and ordinary community infections belong in the differential. A positive low-specificity test should not prevent tissue diagnosis when the clinical picture is inconsistent.
