slides.title: Mucosal, enteric, neurologic, and related infections need distinct diagnostic pathways
slides.section: Mucosal, enteric, neurologic, and related infections need distinct diagnostic pathways
rows: Syphilis, including ocular or neurologic disease
Interpret treponemal/nontreponemal tests with prior treatment and symptoms. Stage-appropriate therapy generally matches treatment without HIV.

Ocular, otic, or neurologic disease changes evaluation and treatment. Neurosyphilis uses aqueous penicillin G 18-24 million units/day IV for 10-14 days; benzathine penicillin alone is inadequate. [28]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Mucosal, enteric, neurologic, and related infections need distinct diagnostic pathways Additional OIs and related infections Syndrome Diagnosis and treatment Decision that changes management Esophageal candidiasis Systemic fluconazole, 200 mg loading then 100-200 mg daily (up to 400 mg), for 14-21 days. Oral suspension can help swallowing. No improvement within about 7 days warrants endoscopy, culture/speciation, and biopsy for CMV/HSV or another cause. Topical therapy is inadequate. [21] Cryptosporidiosis Stool antigen, PCR, or appropriate stain; rehydration, electrolyte replacement, and effective ART are central. Nitazoxanide 500-1,000 mg twice daily with food for ≥14 days may be considered. Drug evidence in advanced HIV is limited. Do not substitute antiparasitic therapy for immune restoration. [22] Cystoisosporiasis Request appropriate stool testing; routine multiplex panels may omit it. TMP-SMX DS twice daily for 7 days or four times daily for 10 days. Persistent disease may need longer/higher-dose treatment; maintenance TMP-SMX is used with CD4 <200. [23] Microsporidiosis Special stool studies or tissue testing; ART and supportive care. Treatment depends on species. Albendazole is active for several species but is unreliable for Enterocytozoon bieneusi; confirm species and specialist access options. [24] PML Progressive focal deficits, characteristic white-matter MRI lesions, and CSF JCV PCR. Repeat testing or biopsy if suspicion remains despite negative PCR. Initiate effective ART immediately. No established JCV-directed antiviral treatment; edema-producing PML-IRIS may require steroids. [20] Severe HSV or disseminated VZV Lesion PCR and organ-directed testing. Severe HSV often requires IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours; extensive/disseminated VZV also requires IV therapy. Adjust for renal function, hydrate, assess CNS/ocular involvement. Nonhealing HSV despite therapy raises resistance; obtain culture/susceptibility and expert treatment. [25] [26] Bacterial pneumonia or sepsis Standard syndrome-based cultures, imaging, resuscitation, and antibiotics. Broaden for documented resistant-organism risk or severe disease. HIV alone does not justify indefinite MRSA or antipseudomonal therapy. Consider simultaneous PCP/TB and obtain source control when needed. [27] Syphilis, including ocular or neurologic disease Interpret treponemal/nontreponemal tests with prior treatment and symptoms. Stage-appropriate therapy generally matches treatment without HIV. Ocular, otic, or neurologic disease changes evaluation and treatment. Neurosyphilis uses aqueous penicillin G 18-24 million units/day IV for 10-14 days; benzathine penicillin alone is inadequate. [28] Kaposi sarcoma, lymphoma, medication toxicity, inflammatory disease, and ordinary community infections belong in the differential. A positive low-specificity test should not prevent tissue diagnosis when the clinical picture is inconsistent.

slides.title: Separate prevention of a first OI from suppression after treatment
slides.section: Separate prevention of a first OI from suppression after treatment
rows: PCP: not on ART or starting ART with CD4 <200
TMP-SMX DS or SS daily; DS daily also preferred if Toxoplasma prophylaxis is needed.

Usually stop when CD4 ≥200 for ≥3 months on ART. Consider stopping at 100-200 only with sustained undetectable RNA for 3-6 months. For patients on ART, restart if CD4 <100 regardless of RNA, or 100-200 with consistently detectable RNA. [6]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Separate prevention of a first OI from suppression after treatment Primary prophylaxis and screening Situation Action Stopping or reassessing PCP: not on ART or starting ART with CD4 <200 TMP-SMX DS or SS daily; DS daily also preferred if Toxoplasma prophylaxis is needed. Usually stop when CD4 ≥200 for ≥3 months on ART. Consider stopping at 100-200 only with sustained undetectable RNA for 3-6 months. For patients on ART, restart if CD4 <100 regardless of RNA, or 100-200 with consistently detectable RNA. [6] Toxoplasma IgG positive and CD4 <100 TMP-SMX DS daily. Dapsone alone and aerosolized pentamidine do not provide Toxoplasma protection. Primary prophylaxis can stop after CD4 >200 for >3 months with sustained suppression. At CD4 100-200, stopping can be considered after HIV RNA remains undetectable for 3-6 months. These criteria do not apply to secondary prophylaxis. [5] CD4 <50 and no effective ART or persistent viremia Give MAC prophylaxis, commonly azithromycin 1,200 mg weekly, when these criteria are met and active MAC has been excluded. Not recommended when immediately starting effective ART. If mycobacterial blood culture is obtained to exclude disease, wait for the result before prophylaxis. [17] New HIV diagnosis and CD4 ≤200 Screen serum CrAg, particularly if CD4 ≤50. Positive antigen requires assessment for CNS disease and treatment. No routine fluconazole primary prophylaxis in U.S. patients with negative CrAg. [7] Low CD4 in a Histoplasma-endemic region Exposure reduction and rapid ART. Itraconazole primary prophylaxis is reserved for CD4 <150 plus high-risk occupational exposure or a community incidence >10 cases per 100 person-years. Residence in Missouri alone is not a blanket indication for itraconazole. [19] CD4 <100 or visual symptoms Baseline retinal examination at <100; urgent ophthalmology for visual change. Do not use routine CMV blood PCR surveillance or valganciclovir prophylaxis. [18] Secondary suppression stopping criteria Prior disease When stopping may be appropriate PCP Usually CD4 ≥200 for ≥3 months on ART; selected patients with CD4 100-200 and sustained viral suppression may qualify. If PCP developed at CD4 >200 while on ART, prophylaxis is generally lifelong. [6] Toxoplasma encephalitis Completed acute therapy, asymptomatic, CD4 >200 for >6 months on ART. [5] Cryptococcosis At least 1 year of antifungals, asymptomatic, CD4 ≥100 and suppressed HIV RNA. [7] Disseminated MAC At least 12 months of treatment, no symptoms, CD4 >100 for ≥6 months on ART. [17] CMV retinitis At least 3 months of treatment, inactive retinal lesions, CD4 ≥100 for ≥3 months; ophthalmology-directed decision and surveillance. [18] Histoplasmosis Azole treatment >1 year, negative fungal blood cultures, antigen below quantification, undetectable HIV RNA, CD4 ≥150, and ART for ≥6 months. [19] After an OI, write the maintenance drug, dose, minimum treatment duration, immune-recovery criteria, and who may stop it. PCP, toxoplasmosis, cryptococcosis, MAC, CMV retinitis, and histoplasmosis do not share one stopping rule. [6] [5] [7] [17] [18] [19]

slides.title: Separate prevention of a first OI from suppression after treatment
slides.section: Separate prevention of a first OI from suppression after treatment
rows: TMP-SMX DS daily. Dapsone alone and aerosolized pentamidine do not provide Toxoplasma protection.

Primary prophylaxis can stop after CD4 >200 for >3 months with sustained suppression. At CD4 100-200, stopping can be considered after HIV RNA remains undetectable for 3-6 months. These criteria do not apply to secondary prophylaxis. [5]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Separate prevention of a first OI from suppression after treatment Primary prophylaxis and screening Situation Action Stopping or reassessing PCP: not on ART or starting ART with CD4 <200 TMP-SMX DS or SS daily; DS daily also preferred if Toxoplasma prophylaxis is needed. Usually stop when CD4 ≥200 for ≥3 months on ART. Consider stopping at 100-200 only with sustained undetectable RNA for 3-6 months. For patients on ART, restart if CD4 <100 regardless of RNA, or 100-200 with consistently detectable RNA. [6] Toxoplasma IgG positive and CD4 <100 TMP-SMX DS daily. Dapsone alone and aerosolized pentamidine do not provide Toxoplasma protection. Primary prophylaxis can stop after CD4 >200 for >3 months with sustained suppression. At CD4 100-200, stopping can be considered after HIV RNA remains undetectable for 3-6 months. These criteria do not apply to secondary prophylaxis. [5] CD4 <50 and no effective ART or persistent viremia Give MAC prophylaxis, commonly azithromycin 1,200 mg weekly, when these criteria are met and active MAC has been excluded. Not recommended when immediately starting effective ART. If mycobacterial blood culture is obtained to exclude disease, wait for the result before prophylaxis. [17] New HIV diagnosis and CD4 ≤200 Screen serum CrAg, particularly if CD4 ≤50. Positive antigen requires assessment for CNS disease and treatment. No routine fluconazole primary prophylaxis in U.S. patients with negative CrAg. [7] Low CD4 in a Histoplasma-endemic region Exposure reduction and rapid ART. Itraconazole primary prophylaxis is reserved for CD4 <150 plus high-risk occupational exposure or a community incidence >10 cases per 100 person-years. Residence in Missouri alone is not a blanket indication for itraconazole. [19] CD4 <100 or visual symptoms Baseline retinal examination at <100; urgent ophthalmology for visual change. Do not use routine CMV blood PCR surveillance or valganciclovir prophylaxis. [18] Secondary suppression stopping criteria Prior disease When stopping may be appropriate PCP Usually CD4 ≥200 for ≥3 months on ART; selected patients with CD4 100-200 and sustained viral suppression may qualify. If PCP developed at CD4 >200 while on ART, prophylaxis is generally lifelong. [6] Toxoplasma encephalitis Completed acute therapy, asymptomatic, CD4 >200 for >6 months on ART. [5] Cryptococcosis At least 1 year of antifungals, asymptomatic, CD4 ≥100 and suppressed HIV RNA. [7] Disseminated MAC At least 12 months of treatment, no symptoms, CD4 >100 for ≥6 months on ART. [17] CMV retinitis At least 3 months of treatment, inactive retinal lesions, CD4 ≥100 for ≥3 months; ophthalmology-directed decision and surveillance. [18] Histoplasmosis Azole treatment >1 year, negative fungal blood cultures, antigen below quantification, undetectable HIV RNA, CD4 ≥150, and ART for ≥6 months. [19] After an OI, write the maintenance drug, dose, minimum treatment duration, immune-recovery criteria, and who may stop it. PCP, toxoplasmosis, cryptococcosis, MAC, CMV retinitis, and histoplasmosis do not share one stopping rule. [6] [5] [7] [17] [18] [19]

slides.title: Separate prevention of a first OI from suppression after treatment
slides.section: Separate prevention of a first OI from suppression after treatment
rows: Low CD4 in a Histoplasma-endemic region
Exposure reduction and rapid ART. Itraconazole primary prophylaxis is reserved for CD4 <150 plus high-risk occupational exposure or a community incidence >10 cases per 100 person-years.
Residence in Missouri alone is not a blanket indication for itraconazole. [19]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Separate prevention of a first OI from suppression after treatment Primary prophylaxis and screening Situation Action Stopping or reassessing PCP: not on ART or starting ART with CD4 <200 TMP-SMX DS or SS daily; DS daily also preferred if Toxoplasma prophylaxis is needed. Usually stop when CD4 ≥200 for ≥3 months on ART. Consider stopping at 100-200 only with sustained undetectable RNA for 3-6 months. For patients on ART, restart if CD4 <100 regardless of RNA, or 100-200 with consistently detectable RNA. [6] Toxoplasma IgG positive and CD4 <100 TMP-SMX DS daily. Dapsone alone and aerosolized pentamidine do not provide Toxoplasma protection. Primary prophylaxis can stop after CD4 >200 for >3 months with sustained suppression. At CD4 100-200, stopping can be considered after HIV RNA remains undetectable for 3-6 months. These criteria do not apply to secondary prophylaxis. [5] CD4 <50 and no effective ART or persistent viremia Give MAC prophylaxis, commonly azithromycin 1,200 mg weekly, when these criteria are met and active MAC has been excluded. Not recommended when immediately starting effective ART. If mycobacterial blood culture is obtained to exclude disease, wait for the result before prophylaxis. [17] New HIV diagnosis and CD4 ≤200 Screen serum CrAg, particularly if CD4 ≤50. Positive antigen requires assessment for CNS disease and treatment. No routine fluconazole primary prophylaxis in U.S. patients with negative CrAg. [7] Low CD4 in a Histoplasma-endemic region Exposure reduction and rapid ART. Itraconazole primary prophylaxis is reserved for CD4 <150 plus high-risk occupational exposure or a community incidence >10 cases per 100 person-years. Residence in Missouri alone is not a blanket indication for itraconazole. [19] CD4 <100 or visual symptoms Baseline retinal examination at <100; urgent ophthalmology for visual change. Do not use routine CMV blood PCR surveillance or valganciclovir prophylaxis. [18] Secondary suppression stopping criteria Prior disease When stopping may be appropriate PCP Usually CD4 ≥200 for ≥3 months on ART; selected patients with CD4 100-200 and sustained viral suppression may qualify. If PCP developed at CD4 >200 while on ART, prophylaxis is generally lifelong. [6] Toxoplasma encephalitis Completed acute therapy, asymptomatic, CD4 >200 for >6 months on ART. [5] Cryptococcosis At least 1 year of antifungals, asymptomatic, CD4 ≥100 and suppressed HIV RNA. [7] Disseminated MAC At least 12 months of treatment, no symptoms, CD4 >100 for ≥6 months on ART. [17] CMV retinitis At least 3 months of treatment, inactive retinal lesions, CD4 ≥100 for ≥3 months; ophthalmology-directed decision and surveillance. [18] Histoplasmosis Azole treatment >1 year, negative fungal blood cultures, antigen below quantification, undetectable HIV RNA, CD4 ≥150, and ART for ≥6 months. [19] After an OI, write the maintenance drug, dose, minimum treatment duration, immune-recovery criteria, and who may stop it. PCP, toxoplasmosis, cryptococcosis, MAC, CMV retinitis, and histoplasmosis do not share one stopping rule. [6] [5] [7] [17] [18] [19]

slides.title: Separate prevention of a first OI from suppression after treatment
slides.section: Separate prevention of a first OI from suppression after treatment
rows: Completed acute therapy, asymptomatic, CD4 >200 for >6 months on ART. [5]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Separate prevention of a first OI from suppression after treatment Primary prophylaxis and screening Situation Action Stopping or reassessing PCP: not on ART or starting ART with CD4 <200 TMP-SMX DS or SS daily; DS daily also preferred if Toxoplasma prophylaxis is needed. Usually stop when CD4 ≥200 for ≥3 months on ART. Consider stopping at 100-200 only with sustained undetectable RNA for 3-6 months. For patients on ART, restart if CD4 <100 regardless of RNA, or 100-200 with consistently detectable RNA. [6] Toxoplasma IgG positive and CD4 <100 TMP-SMX DS daily. Dapsone alone and aerosolized pentamidine do not provide Toxoplasma protection. Primary prophylaxis can stop after CD4 >200 for >3 months with sustained suppression. At CD4 100-200, stopping can be considered after HIV RNA remains undetectable for 3-6 months. These criteria do not apply to secondary prophylaxis. [5] CD4 <50 and no effective ART or persistent viremia Give MAC prophylaxis, commonly azithromycin 1,200 mg weekly, when these criteria are met and active MAC has been excluded. Not recommended when immediately starting effective ART. If mycobacterial blood culture is obtained to exclude disease, wait for the result before prophylaxis. [17] New HIV diagnosis and CD4 ≤200 Screen serum CrAg, particularly if CD4 ≤50. Positive antigen requires assessment for CNS disease and treatment. No routine fluconazole primary prophylaxis in U.S. patients with negative CrAg. [7] Low CD4 in a Histoplasma-endemic region Exposure reduction and rapid ART. Itraconazole primary prophylaxis is reserved for CD4 <150 plus high-risk occupational exposure or a community incidence >10 cases per 100 person-years. Residence in Missouri alone is not a blanket indication for itraconazole. [19] CD4 <100 or visual symptoms Baseline retinal examination at <100; urgent ophthalmology for visual change. Do not use routine CMV blood PCR surveillance or valganciclovir prophylaxis. [18] Secondary suppression stopping criteria Prior disease When stopping may be appropriate PCP Usually CD4 ≥200 for ≥3 months on ART; selected patients with CD4 100-200 and sustained viral suppression may qualify. If PCP developed at CD4 >200 while on ART, prophylaxis is generally lifelong. [6] Toxoplasma encephalitis Completed acute therapy, asymptomatic, CD4 >200 for >6 months on ART. [5] Cryptococcosis At least 1 year of antifungals, asymptomatic, CD4 ≥100 and suppressed HIV RNA. [7] Disseminated MAC At least 12 months of treatment, no symptoms, CD4 >100 for ≥6 months on ART. [17] CMV retinitis At least 3 months of treatment, inactive retinal lesions, CD4 ≥100 for ≥3 months; ophthalmology-directed decision and surveillance. [18] Histoplasmosis Azole treatment >1 year, negative fungal blood cultures, antigen below quantification, undetectable HIV RNA, CD4 ≥150, and ART for ≥6 months. [19] After an OI, write the maintenance drug, dose, minimum treatment duration, immune-recovery criteria, and who may stop it. PCP, toxoplasmosis, cryptococcosis, MAC, CMV retinitis, and histoplasmosis do not share one stopping rule. [6] [5] [7] [17] [18] [19]

slides.title: Separate prevention of a first OI from suppression after treatment
slides.section: Separate prevention of a first OI from suppression after treatment
rows: At least 3 months of treatment, inactive retinal lesions, CD4 ≥100 for ≥3 months; ophthalmology-directed decision and surveillance. [18]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Separate prevention of a first OI from suppression after treatment Primary prophylaxis and screening Situation Action Stopping or reassessing PCP: not on ART or starting ART with CD4 <200 TMP-SMX DS or SS daily; DS daily also preferred if Toxoplasma prophylaxis is needed. Usually stop when CD4 ≥200 for ≥3 months on ART. Consider stopping at 100-200 only with sustained undetectable RNA for 3-6 months. For patients on ART, restart if CD4 <100 regardless of RNA, or 100-200 with consistently detectable RNA. [6] Toxoplasma IgG positive and CD4 <100 TMP-SMX DS daily. Dapsone alone and aerosolized pentamidine do not provide Toxoplasma protection. Primary prophylaxis can stop after CD4 >200 for >3 months with sustained suppression. At CD4 100-200, stopping can be considered after HIV RNA remains undetectable for 3-6 months. These criteria do not apply to secondary prophylaxis. [5] CD4 <50 and no effective ART or persistent viremia Give MAC prophylaxis, commonly azithromycin 1,200 mg weekly, when these criteria are met and active MAC has been excluded. Not recommended when immediately starting effective ART. If mycobacterial blood culture is obtained to exclude disease, wait for the result before prophylaxis. [17] New HIV diagnosis and CD4 ≤200 Screen serum CrAg, particularly if CD4 ≤50. Positive antigen requires assessment for CNS disease and treatment. No routine fluconazole primary prophylaxis in U.S. patients with negative CrAg. [7] Low CD4 in a Histoplasma-endemic region Exposure reduction and rapid ART. Itraconazole primary prophylaxis is reserved for CD4 <150 plus high-risk occupational exposure or a community incidence >10 cases per 100 person-years. Residence in Missouri alone is not a blanket indication for itraconazole. [19] CD4 <100 or visual symptoms Baseline retinal examination at <100; urgent ophthalmology for visual change. Do not use routine CMV blood PCR surveillance or valganciclovir prophylaxis. [18] Secondary suppression stopping criteria Prior disease When stopping may be appropriate PCP Usually CD4 ≥200 for ≥3 months on ART; selected patients with CD4 100-200 and sustained viral suppression may qualify. If PCP developed at CD4 >200 while on ART, prophylaxis is generally lifelong. [6] Toxoplasma encephalitis Completed acute therapy, asymptomatic, CD4 >200 for >6 months on ART. [5] Cryptococcosis At least 1 year of antifungals, asymptomatic, CD4 ≥100 and suppressed HIV RNA. [7] Disseminated MAC At least 12 months of treatment, no symptoms, CD4 >100 for ≥6 months on ART. [17] CMV retinitis At least 3 months of treatment, inactive retinal lesions, CD4 ≥100 for ≥3 months; ophthalmology-directed decision and surveillance. [18] Histoplasmosis Azole treatment >1 year, negative fungal blood cultures, antigen below quantification, undetectable HIV RNA, CD4 ≥150, and ART for ≥6 months. [19] After an OI, write the maintenance drug, dose, minimum treatment duration, immune-recovery criteria, and who may stop it. PCP, toxoplasmosis, cryptococcosis, MAC, CMV retinitis, and histoplasmosis do not share one stopping rule. [6] [5] [7] [17] [18] [19]

slides.title: Clinical worsening after ART is a diagnostic problem before it is an IRIS diagnosis
slides.section: Clinical worsening after ART is a diagnostic problem before it is an IRIS diagnosis
paragraphs: Unmasking IRIS reveals previously unrecognized infection; paradoxical IRIS worsens a treated infection after immune recovery begins. Reassess adherence, drug exposure, resistance, source control, toxicity, and a second process. The timing and a falling HIV RNA support the context but do not prove IRIS. [3] [7] [17] [5]

Usually continue ART and active antimicrobial treatment while investigating. Mild disease may need symptomatic treatment; severe, organ-threatening inflammation may need corticosteroids and expert management. CNS disease requires particular care. Do not use steroids before considering uncontrolled infection or malignancy. [3] [7] [20]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Clinical worsening after ART is a diagnostic problem before it is an IRIS diagnosis Unmasking IRIS reveals previously unrecognized infection; paradoxical IRIS worsens a treated infection after immune recovery begins. Reassess adherence, drug exposure, resistance, source control, toxicity, and a second process. The timing and a falling HIV RNA support the context but do not prove IRIS. [3] [7] [17] [5] Usually continue ART and active antimicrobial treatment while investigating. Mild disease may need symptomatic treatment; severe, organ-threatening inflammation may need corticosteroids and expert management. CNS disease requires particular care. Do not use steroids before considering uncontrolled infection or malignancy. [3] [7] [20] Fellow and attending discussion In cryptococcal deterioration, repeat LP with opening pressure and fungal culture. Persistent antigen does not establish microbiologic failure. In apparent toxoplasmosis, steroid-responsive lymphoma can mislead. In MAC, lymphadenitis after ART may reflect IRIS but still requires the clinical and microbiologic context. [7] [5] [17]

slides.title: Prevention includes PrEP, time-sensitive PEP, and sustained viral suppression
slides.section: Prevention includes PrEP, time-sensitive PEP, and sustained viral suppression
rows: Daily oral PrEP for sexual and injection-related risk
Assess renal function, HBV status, HIV testing, and adherence.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Prevention includes PrEP, time-sensitive PEP, and sustained viral suppression PrEP choices Option Schedule and use Required safeguards FTC/TDF Daily oral PrEP for sexual and injection-related risk Assess renal function, HBV status, HIV testing, and adherence. FTC/TAF Daily oral PrEP for sexual risk excluding receptive vaginal exposure Review renal function, weight/lipids, HBV, and the population studied. Cabotegravir IM initiation, second dose at 1 month, then every 2 months Antigen-antibody plus HIV RNA testing; plan for missed injections and the long drug tail. Lenacapavir Every 6 months SC after oral loading; approved for eligible adults/adolescents ≥35 kg Use the current PrEP label and CDC testing schedule. Exclude acute HIV; review interactions and a missed-dose/tail plan. [29] [30] [31] Oral PrEP requires renal eligibility and serial HIV testing; FTC/TDF generally needs eCrCl ≥60 mL/min and FTC/TAF ≥30. Injectable PrEP avoids tenofovir renal exposure but still requires reliable testing and return visits. Never use a prevention-only regimen as HIV treatment. [29] [30] For a substantial nonoccupational exposure, start PEP as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours and no later than 72 hours, for 28 days. Do not wait for pending source testing. Preferred adult options include BIC/FTC/TAF or DTG plus an appropriate tenofovir/FTC or 3TC backbone. Obtain baseline testing, contact at about 24 hours, and antigen-antibody plus NAT follow-up at 4-6 and 12 weeks after exposure under the CDC algorithm. Plan direct PEP-to-PrEP transition if risk continues. Occupational exposures follow the employee-health pathway. [32] Sustained HIV RNA <200 copies/mL on ART prevents sexual HIV transmission (U=U). It does not prevent other STIs and should not be extrapolated to zero risk for breastfeeding or shared injection equipment. For patients starting ART, use another prevention method for at least 6 months and until HIV RNA <200 is documented; confirm sustained suppression. Support ongoing ART access. [33]

slides.title: Prevention includes PrEP, time-sensitive PEP, and sustained viral suppression
slides.section: Prevention includes PrEP, time-sensitive PEP, and sustained viral suppression
paragraphs: For a substantial nonoccupational exposure, start PEP as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours and no later than 72 hours, for 28 days. Do not wait for pending source testing. Preferred adult options include BIC/FTC/TAF or DTG plus an appropriate tenofovir/FTC or 3TC backbone. Obtain baseline testing, contact at about 24 hours, and antigen-antibody plus NAT follow-up at 4-6 and 12 weeks after exposure under the CDC algorithm. Plan direct PEP-to-PrEP transition if risk continues. Occupational exposures follow the employee-health pathway. [32]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Prevention includes PrEP, time-sensitive PEP, and sustained viral suppression PrEP choices Option Schedule and use Required safeguards FTC/TDF Daily oral PrEP for sexual and injection-related risk Assess renal function, HBV status, HIV testing, and adherence. FTC/TAF Daily oral PrEP for sexual risk excluding receptive vaginal exposure Review renal function, weight/lipids, HBV, and the population studied. Cabotegravir IM initiation, second dose at 1 month, then every 2 months Antigen-antibody plus HIV RNA testing; plan for missed injections and the long drug tail. Lenacapavir Every 6 months SC after oral loading; approved for eligible adults/adolescents ≥35 kg Use the current PrEP label and CDC testing schedule. Exclude acute HIV; review interactions and a missed-dose/tail plan. [29] [30] [31] Oral PrEP requires renal eligibility and serial HIV testing; FTC/TDF generally needs eCrCl ≥60 mL/min and FTC/TAF ≥30. Injectable PrEP avoids tenofovir renal exposure but still requires reliable testing and return visits. Never use a prevention-only regimen as HIV treatment. [29] [30] For a substantial nonoccupational exposure, start PEP as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours and no later than 72 hours, for 28 days. Do not wait for pending source testing. Preferred adult options include BIC/FTC/TAF or DTG plus an appropriate tenofovir/FTC or 3TC backbone. Obtain baseline testing, contact at about 24 hours, and antigen-antibody plus NAT follow-up at 4-6 and 12 weeks after exposure under the CDC algorithm. Plan direct PEP-to-PrEP transition if risk continues. Occupational exposures follow the employee-health pathway. [32] Sustained HIV RNA <200 copies/mL on ART prevents sexual HIV transmission (U=U). It does not prevent other STIs and should not be extrapolated to zero risk for breastfeeding or shared injection equipment. For patients starting ART, use another prevention method for at least 6 months and until HIV RNA <200 is documented; confirm sustained suppression. Support ongoing ART access. [33]

slides.title: Suppression is the beginning of durable HIV care
slides.section: Suppression is the beginning of durable HIV care
paragraphs: Review vaccination history, hepatitis prevention/treatment, STI screening, cancer screening, smoking, blood pressure, metabolic health, bone health, mental health, and substance use. Coordinate HIV-specific cervical and anal screening pathways with available follow-up services. [4] [34]

Use current HIV immunization guidance for influenza, COVID-19, pneumococcal, hepatitis A/B, meningococcal, HPV, recombinant zoster, and exposure-based mpox vaccination. Live MMR and varicella vaccines require adequate immune status; avoid at CD4 <200 and assess pregnancy. Check HBV vaccine response when indicated. [34]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Suppression is the beginning of durable HIV care Review vaccination history, hepatitis prevention/treatment, STI screening, cancer screening, smoking, blood pressure, metabolic health, bone health, mental health, and substance use. Coordinate HIV-specific cervical and anal screening pathways with available follow-up services. [4] [34] Use current HIV immunization guidance for influenza, COVID-19, pneumococcal, hepatitis A/B, meningococcal, HPV, recombinant zoster, and exposure-based mpox vaccination. Live MMR and varicella vaccines require adequate immune status; avoid at CD4 <200 and assess pregnancy. Check HBV vaccine response when indicated. [34] Current ACC/AHA multisociety guidance, endorsed by the May 2026 NIH statement, recommends statin primary prevention for people with HIV aged 40-75. Choose the statin and intensity using cardiovascular risk and ART interactions. [35] A patient leaving with an ART prescription but no way to obtain it does not have a completed discharge plan. Confirm supply through the first outpatient visit, an actual appointment, pending-result ownership, and a contingency if a dose or visit is missed.

slides.title: Suppression is the beginning of durable HIV care
slides.section: Suppression is the beginning of durable HIV care
paragraphs: Current ACC/AHA multisociety guidance, endorsed by the May 2026 NIH statement, recommends statin primary prevention for people with HIV aged 40-75. Choose the statin and intensity using cardiovascular risk and ART interactions. [35]

A patient leaving with an ART prescription but no way to obtain it does not have a completed discharge plan. Confirm supply through the first outpatient visit, an actual appointment, pending-result ownership, and a contingency if a dose or visit is missed.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Suppression is the beginning of durable HIV care Review vaccination history, hepatitis prevention/treatment, STI screening, cancer screening, smoking, blood pressure, metabolic health, bone health, mental health, and substance use. Coordinate HIV-specific cervical and anal screening pathways with available follow-up services. [4] [34] Use current HIV immunization guidance for influenza, COVID-19, pneumococcal, hepatitis A/B, meningococcal, HPV, recombinant zoster, and exposure-based mpox vaccination. Live MMR and varicella vaccines require adequate immune status; avoid at CD4 <200 and assess pregnancy. Check HBV vaccine response when indicated. [34] Current ACC/AHA multisociety guidance, endorsed by the May 2026 NIH statement, recommends statin primary prevention for people with HIV aged 40-75. Choose the statin and intensity using cardiovascular risk and ART interactions. [35] A patient leaving with an ART prescription but no way to obtain it does not have a completed discharge plan. Confirm supply through the first outpatient visit, an actual appointment, pending-result ownership, and a contingency if a dose or visit is missed.

slides.title: New options expand delivery choices but do not remove eligibility requirements
slides.section: New options expand delivery choices but do not remove eligibility requirements
paragraphs: Long-acting CAB/RPV is a complete injectable maintenance regimen given monthly or every 2 months for appropriately selected patients, generally with HIV RNA <50 for at least 3 months. Review suppression, all resistance and failure history, HBV treatment, pregnancy, interactions, and ability to attend injections. A written bridging and missed-dose plan is part of prescribing. LATITUDE adds evidence for patients with prior adherence challenges after an initial supported oral-treatment phase. [36] [37] [38]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
New options expand delivery choices but do not remove eligibility requirements Long-acting CAB/RPV is a complete injectable maintenance regimen given monthly or every 2 months for appropriately selected patients, generally with HIV RNA <50 for at least 3 months. Review suppression, all resistance and failure history, HBV treatment, pregnancy, interactions, and ability to attend injections. A written bridging and missed-dose plan is part of prescribing. LATITUDE adds evidence for patients with prior adherence challenges after an initial supported oral-treatment phase. [36] [37] [38] Lenacapavir has separate prevention and treatment roles. Yeztugo is the prevention product. Sunlenca is used with other active antiretrovirals in heavily treatment-experienced adults with multidrug-resistant HIV; it is not stand-alone treatment or routine initial ART. A long pharmacologic tail can expose virus to functional monotherapy when companion drugs or visits are missed. [31] [39] Doravirine/islatravir (Idvynso), approved in April 2026, is a once-daily 100/0.25 mg two-drug switch regimen for suppressed adults on stable ART without prior virologic treatment failure or known doravirine resistance substitutions. It is not a rapid-start regimen. Strong CYP3A inducers and concomitant 3TC/FTC are contraindicated; it does not provide an HBV treatment backbone. [40] Fellow and attending discussion When discussing an investigational strategy, specify the population, stage of development, comparator, and outcome. Longer dosing intervals are not themselves evidence of better clinical outcomes, a cure, or an adequate resistance barrier. The selected updates here are not an exhaustive pipeline review.

slides.title: START established the benefit of treatment at high CD4 counts
slides.section: Read the endpoint and population before applying a trial
paragraphs: 2015 · Randomized trial · 4,685 adults
Immediate ART versus deferral in asymptomatic adults with CD4 >500. Serious AIDS/non-AIDS events or death occurred in 1.8% versus 4.1%; HR 0.43, 95% CI 0.30-0.62. [41]
Supports treating all people with HIV. It does not answer ART timing during cryptococcal meningitis.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Read the endpoint and population before applying a trial START established the benefit of treatment at high CD4 counts 2015 · Randomized trial · 4,685 adults Immediate ART versus deferral in asymptomatic adults with CD4 >500. Serious AIDS/non-AIDS events or death occurred in 1.8% versus 4.1%; HR 0.43, 95% CI 0.30-0.62. [41] Supports treating all people with HIV. It does not answer ART timing during cryptococcal meningitis. A5164 supports early ART in many acute OIs 2009 · Randomized strategy trial · 282 participants Early ART at median 12 days versus deferred ART at median 45 days. AIDS progression/death occurred in 14% versus 24%; this was a secondary outcome, and the primary ordered endpoint was not significantly different. [42] Most participants had PCP; TB was excluded. Do not generalize the average result to every CNS infection. COAT demonstrates why cryptococcal meningitis is an exception 2014 · Randomized trial · 177 adults ART at 1-2 weeks versus approximately 5 weeks after diagnosis. Mortality at 26 weeks was 45% versus 30%; HR 1.73, 95% CI 1.06-2.82. [43] Early immune restoration can harm in this setting. Antifungal regimens and care setting affect applicability, but the trial supports delayed ART. REPRIEVE supports cardiovascular prevention during treated HIV 2023 · Randomized trial · 7,769 participants Pitavastatin 4 mg daily versus placebo in treated HIV with low-to-moderate cardiovascular risk. MACE rates were 4.81 versus 7.32 per 1,000 person-years; HR 0.65, 95% CI 0.48-0.90. [44] Muscle symptoms and diabetes were more frequent with pitavastatin. Use current prevention guidance and interaction checks rather than extrapolating one dose to every statin. PURPOSE 1 established strong preventive efficacy in young women 2024 · Randomized phase 3 trial No incident HIV infections among 2,134 receiving lenacapavir in the primary analysis; incidence 0 per 100 person-years, 95% CI 0-0.19. Oral FTC/TAF and FTC/TDF groups had infections. [45] The zero-event finding is an observed trial result, not a guarantee of lifelong or perfect protection. Oral adherence and modeled background incidence matter to interpretation. PURPOSE 2 extends preventive evidence to men and gender-diverse people 2024 online publication · Randomized phase 3 trial Two infections in the lenacapavir arm and nine with FTC/TDF in the primary report. The incidence ratio versus estimated background incidence was 0.04 (95% CI 0.01-0.18); versus FTC/TDF, 0.11 (0.02-0.51). [46] Background incidence is not a randomized untreated control. Breakthrough infection and capsid resistance remain possible. LATITUDE supports monthly injections after a supported oral phase 2026 · Randomized open-label trial · 453 enrolled in step 1; 306 randomized in step 2 Participants who achieved HIV RNA ≤200 during supported oral treatment could be randomized. Week-48 regimen failure was 22.8% with CAB/RPV versus 41.2% with oral standard care; difference -18.4 percentage points, 98.4% CI -32.4 to -4.3. [38] The endpoint includes virologic failure or permanent discontinuation. This was not immediate injectable treatment of all unsuppressed patients, and the care support is part of applicability. Trial summaries use the linked original publications or indexed abstracts. Full-text access was not available for every trial; no unreviewed subgroup analysis is asserted.

slides.title: LATITUDE supports monthly injections after a supported oral phase
slides.section: Read the endpoint and population before applying a trial
paragraphs: Trial summaries use the linked original publications or indexed abstracts. Full-text access was not available for every trial; no unreviewed subgroup analysis is asserted.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Read the endpoint and population before applying a trial START established the benefit of treatment at high CD4 counts 2015 · Randomized trial · 4,685 adults Immediate ART versus deferral in asymptomatic adults with CD4 >500. Serious AIDS/non-AIDS events or death occurred in 1.8% versus 4.1%; HR 0.43, 95% CI 0.30-0.62. [41] Supports treating all people with HIV. It does not answer ART timing during cryptococcal meningitis. A5164 supports early ART in many acute OIs 2009 · Randomized strategy trial · 282 participants Early ART at median 12 days versus deferred ART at median 45 days. AIDS progression/death occurred in 14% versus 24%; this was a secondary outcome, and the primary ordered endpoint was not significantly different. [42] Most participants had PCP; TB was excluded. Do not generalize the average result to every CNS infection. COAT demonstrates why cryptococcal meningitis is an exception 2014 · Randomized trial · 177 adults ART at 1-2 weeks versus approximately 5 weeks after diagnosis. Mortality at 26 weeks was 45% versus 30%; HR 1.73, 95% CI 1.06-2.82. [43] Early immune restoration can harm in this setting. Antifungal regimens and care setting affect applicability, but the trial supports delayed ART. REPRIEVE supports cardiovascular prevention during treated HIV 2023 · Randomized trial · 7,769 participants Pitavastatin 4 mg daily versus placebo in treated HIV with low-to-moderate cardiovascular risk. MACE rates were 4.81 versus 7.32 per 1,000 person-years; HR 0.65, 95% CI 0.48-0.90. [44] Muscle symptoms and diabetes were more frequent with pitavastatin. Use current prevention guidance and interaction checks rather than extrapolating one dose to every statin. PURPOSE 1 established strong preventive efficacy in young women 2024 · Randomized phase 3 trial No incident HIV infections among 2,134 receiving lenacapavir in the primary analysis; incidence 0 per 100 person-years, 95% CI 0-0.19. Oral FTC/TAF and FTC/TDF groups had infections. [45] The zero-event finding is an observed trial result, not a guarantee of lifelong or perfect protection. Oral adherence and modeled background incidence matter to interpretation. PURPOSE 2 extends preventive evidence to men and gender-diverse people 2024 online publication · Randomized phase 3 trial Two infections in the lenacapavir arm and nine with FTC/TDF in the primary report. The incidence ratio versus estimated background incidence was 0.04 (95% CI 0.01-0.18); versus FTC/TDF, 0.11 (0.02-0.51). [46] Background incidence is not a randomized untreated control. Breakthrough infection and capsid resistance remain possible. LATITUDE supports monthly injections after a supported oral phase 2026 · Randomized open-label trial · 453 enrolled in step 1; 306 randomized in step 2 Participants who achieved HIV RNA ≤200 during supported oral treatment could be randomized. Week-48 regimen failure was 22.8% with CAB/RPV versus 41.2% with oral standard care; difference -18.4 percentage points, 98.4% CI -32.4 to -4.3. [38] The endpoint includes virologic failure or permanent discontinuation. This was not immediate injectable treatment of all unsuppressed patients, and the care support is part of applicability. Trial summaries use the linked original publications or indexed abstracts. Full-text access was not available for every trial; no unreviewed subgroup analysis is asserted.

slides.title: Case 1 · An acute viral syndrome with discordant testing
slides.section: Use these cases to practice a defensible next step
paragraphs: A 26-year-old has fever, rash, pharyngitis, a reactive antigen-antibody screen, and negative antibody differentiation.
What is the next test, and what history changes empiric ART?
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Use these cases to practice a defensible next step Case 1 · An acute viral syndrome with discordant testing A 26-year-old has fever, rash, pharyngitis, a reactive antigen-antibody screen, and negative antibody differentiation. What is the next test, and what history changes empiric ART? Discuss the next step Obtain HIV RNA and ask about oral/injectable PrEP and PEP. Repeat an ambiguous result on a new specimen. If HIV followed CAB PrEP, request integrase genotype and use the recommended boosted-darunavir strategy while awaiting results. [1] Case 2 · New HIV with hypoxemic pneumonia A 42-year-old has CD4 38, diffuse ground-glass opacity, and room-air PaO₂ 62 mmHg. What should happen today, and when should ART begin? Discuss the next step Obtain respiratory PCP testing while starting treatment-dose TMP-SMX and adjunctive prednisone. Assess bacterial/TB coinfection and oxygen needs. Plan ART within 2 weeks and subsequent PCP prophylaxis. [6] Case 3 · Headache before rapid ART A 35-year-old with CD4 24 has 2 weeks of headache and a positive serum CrAg. Is same-day ART the next step? Discuss the next step First evaluate CNS disease with LP, including opening pressure and fungal culture, after imaging if indicated. Begin appropriate antifungals and manage pressure. CNS cryptococcosis usually calls for ART deferral around 4-6 weeks. [7] Case 4 · Ring-enhancing lesions that do not improve A patient with CD4 48, positive Toxoplasma IgG, and multiple lesions receives appropriate therapy but is unchanged at day 14. What should prevent automatic extension of empiric therapy? Discuss the next step Reassess exposure and adherence and pursue alternative diagnoses, particularly CNS lymphoma. Discuss biopsy. A presumptive toxoplasma diagnosis should have a defined reassessment point. [5] Case 5 · CMV PCR distracts from the involved organ A patient with CD4 19 has diarrhea and a positive plasma CMV PCR. Does this establish CMV colitis? Discuss the next step No. Obtain a syndrome-directed stool evaluation and consider endoscopy with biopsy. Ask about vision and arrange ophthalmology as indicated. Positive blood PCR does not by itself justify treatment for tissue disease. [18] Case 6 · Fever and cytopenias before MAC prophylaxis A patient newly diagnosed with HIV has CD4 12, fever, weight loss, cytopenias, and elevated alkaline phosphatase. Should weekly azithromycin be started immediately? Discuss the next step Evaluate active MAC and disseminated histoplasmosis, with appropriate cultures, antigen testing, and tissue when needed. MAC prophylaxis can expose active disease to monotherapy. Severe histoplasmosis warrants prompt amphotericin-based treatment. [17] [19] Case 7 · A suppressed patient wants fewer pills A patient with HIV/HBV is suppressed on tenofovir-containing ART and requests CAB/RPV. What cannot be lost in the switch? Discuss the next step HBV treatment. Review resistance and the rest of injectable eligibility, then preserve or separately provide appropriate HBV therapy. CAB/RPV itself does not treat HBV. [12] [36] Case 8 · A new exposure presents overnight An HIV-negative patient presents 18 hours after a substantial sexual exposure; the source result is pending. What action is time sensitive? Discuss the next step Start indicated PEP without waiting, obtain baseline testing, provide the full 28-day plan, and arrange follow-up and a PrEP transition discussion. [32]

slides.title: Case 2 · New HIV with hypoxemic pneumonia
slides.section: Use these cases to practice a defensible next step
paragraphs: A 42-year-old has CD4 38, diffuse ground-glass opacity, and room-air PaO₂ 62 mmHg.
What should happen today, and when should ART begin?
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Use these cases to practice a defensible next step Case 1 · An acute viral syndrome with discordant testing A 26-year-old has fever, rash, pharyngitis, a reactive antigen-antibody screen, and negative antibody differentiation. What is the next test, and what history changes empiric ART? Discuss the next step Obtain HIV RNA and ask about oral/injectable PrEP and PEP. Repeat an ambiguous result on a new specimen. If HIV followed CAB PrEP, request integrase genotype and use the recommended boosted-darunavir strategy while awaiting results. [1] Case 2 · New HIV with hypoxemic pneumonia A 42-year-old has CD4 38, diffuse ground-glass opacity, and room-air PaO₂ 62 mmHg. What should happen today, and when should ART begin? Discuss the next step Obtain respiratory PCP testing while starting treatment-dose TMP-SMX and adjunctive prednisone. Assess bacterial/TB coinfection and oxygen needs. Plan ART within 2 weeks and subsequent PCP prophylaxis. [6] Case 3 · Headache before rapid ART A 35-year-old with CD4 24 has 2 weeks of headache and a positive serum CrAg. Is same-day ART the next step? Discuss the next step First evaluate CNS disease with LP, including opening pressure and fungal culture, after imaging if indicated. Begin appropriate antifungals and manage pressure. CNS cryptococcosis usually calls for ART deferral around 4-6 weeks. [7] Case 4 · Ring-enhancing lesions that do not improve A patient with CD4 48, positive Toxoplasma IgG, and multiple lesions receives appropriate therapy but is unchanged at day 14. What should prevent automatic extension of empiric therapy? Discuss the next step Reassess exposure and adherence and pursue alternative diagnoses, particularly CNS lymphoma. Discuss biopsy. A presumptive toxoplasma diagnosis should have a defined reassessment point. [5] Case 5 · CMV PCR distracts from the involved organ A patient with CD4 19 has diarrhea and a positive plasma CMV PCR. Does this establish CMV colitis? Discuss the next step No. Obtain a syndrome-directed stool evaluation and consider endoscopy with biopsy. Ask about vision and arrange ophthalmology as indicated. Positive blood PCR does not by itself justify treatment for tissue disease. [18] Case 6 · Fever and cytopenias before MAC prophylaxis A patient newly diagnosed with HIV has CD4 12, fever, weight loss, cytopenias, and elevated alkaline phosphatase. Should weekly azithromycin be started immediately? Discuss the next step Evaluate active MAC and disseminated histoplasmosis, with appropriate cultures, antigen testing, and tissue when needed. MAC prophylaxis can expose active disease to monotherapy. Severe histoplasmosis warrants prompt amphotericin-based treatment. [17] [19] Case 7 · A suppressed patient wants fewer pills A patient with HIV/HBV is suppressed on tenofovir-containing ART and requests CAB/RPV. What cannot be lost in the switch? Discuss the next step HBV treatment. Review resistance and the rest of injectable eligibility, then preserve or separately provide appropriate HBV therapy. CAB/RPV itself does not treat HBV. [12] [36] Case 8 · A new exposure presents overnight An HIV-negative patient presents 18 hours after a substantial sexual exposure; the source result is pending. What action is time sensitive? Discuss the next step Start indicated PEP without waiting, obtain baseline testing, provide the full 28-day plan, and arrange follow-up and a PrEP transition discussion. [32]

slides.title: Discuss the next step
slides.section: Use these cases to practice a defensible next step
paragraphs: First evaluate CNS disease with LP, including opening pressure and fungal culture, after imaging if indicated. Begin appropriate antifungals and manage pressure. CNS cryptococcosis usually calls for ART deferral around 4-6 weeks. [7]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Use these cases to practice a defensible next step Case 1 · An acute viral syndrome with discordant testing A 26-year-old has fever, rash, pharyngitis, a reactive antigen-antibody screen, and negative antibody differentiation. What is the next test, and what history changes empiric ART? Discuss the next step Obtain HIV RNA and ask about oral/injectable PrEP and PEP. Repeat an ambiguous result on a new specimen. If HIV followed CAB PrEP, request integrase genotype and use the recommended boosted-darunavir strategy while awaiting results. [1] Case 2 · New HIV with hypoxemic pneumonia A 42-year-old has CD4 38, diffuse ground-glass opacity, and room-air PaO₂ 62 mmHg. What should happen today, and when should ART begin? Discuss the next step Obtain respiratory PCP testing while starting treatment-dose TMP-SMX and adjunctive prednisone. Assess bacterial/TB coinfection and oxygen needs. Plan ART within 2 weeks and subsequent PCP prophylaxis. [6] Case 3 · Headache before rapid ART A 35-year-old with CD4 24 has 2 weeks of headache and a positive serum CrAg. Is same-day ART the next step? Discuss the next step First evaluate CNS disease with LP, including opening pressure and fungal culture, after imaging if indicated. Begin appropriate antifungals and manage pressure. CNS cryptococcosis usually calls for ART deferral around 4-6 weeks. [7] Case 4 · Ring-enhancing lesions that do not improve A patient with CD4 48, positive Toxoplasma IgG, and multiple lesions receives appropriate therapy but is unchanged at day 14. What should prevent automatic extension of empiric therapy? Discuss the next step Reassess exposure and adherence and pursue alternative diagnoses, particularly CNS lymphoma. Discuss biopsy. A presumptive toxoplasma diagnosis should have a defined reassessment point. [5] Case 5 · CMV PCR distracts from the involved organ A patient with CD4 19 has diarrhea and a positive plasma CMV PCR. Does this establish CMV colitis? Discuss the next step No. Obtain a syndrome-directed stool evaluation and consider endoscopy with biopsy. Ask about vision and arrange ophthalmology as indicated. Positive blood PCR does not by itself justify treatment for tissue disease. [18] Case 6 · Fever and cytopenias before MAC prophylaxis A patient newly diagnosed with HIV has CD4 12, fever, weight loss, cytopenias, and elevated alkaline phosphatase. Should weekly azithromycin be started immediately? Discuss the next step Evaluate active MAC and disseminated histoplasmosis, with appropriate cultures, antigen testing, and tissue when needed. MAC prophylaxis can expose active disease to monotherapy. Severe histoplasmosis warrants prompt amphotericin-based treatment. [17] [19] Case 7 · A suppressed patient wants fewer pills A patient with HIV/HBV is suppressed on tenofovir-containing ART and requests CAB/RPV. What cannot be lost in the switch? Discuss the next step HBV treatment. Review resistance and the rest of injectable eligibility, then preserve or separately provide appropriate HBV therapy. CAB/RPV itself does not treat HBV. [12] [36] Case 8 · A new exposure presents overnight An HIV-negative patient presents 18 hours after a substantial sexual exposure; the source result is pending. What action is time sensitive? Discuss the next step Start indicated PEP without waiting, obtain baseline testing, provide the full 28-day plan, and arrange follow-up and a PrEP transition discussion. [32]

slides.title: Case 5 · CMV PCR distracts from the involved organ
slides.section: Use these cases to practice a defensible next step
paragraphs: A patient with CD4 19 has diarrhea and a positive plasma CMV PCR.
Does this establish CMV colitis?
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Use these cases to practice a defensible next step Case 1 · An acute viral syndrome with discordant testing A 26-year-old has fever, rash, pharyngitis, a reactive antigen-antibody screen, and negative antibody differentiation. What is the next test, and what history changes empiric ART? Discuss the next step Obtain HIV RNA and ask about oral/injectable PrEP and PEP. Repeat an ambiguous result on a new specimen. If HIV followed CAB PrEP, request integrase genotype and use the recommended boosted-darunavir strategy while awaiting results. [1] Case 2 · New HIV with hypoxemic pneumonia A 42-year-old has CD4 38, diffuse ground-glass opacity, and room-air PaO₂ 62 mmHg. What should happen today, and when should ART begin? Discuss the next step Obtain respiratory PCP testing while starting treatment-dose TMP-SMX and adjunctive prednisone. Assess bacterial/TB coinfection and oxygen needs. Plan ART within 2 weeks and subsequent PCP prophylaxis. [6] Case 3 · Headache before rapid ART A 35-year-old with CD4 24 has 2 weeks of headache and a positive serum CrAg. Is same-day ART the next step? Discuss the next step First evaluate CNS disease with LP, including opening pressure and fungal culture, after imaging if indicated. Begin appropriate antifungals and manage pressure. CNS cryptococcosis usually calls for ART deferral around 4-6 weeks. [7] Case 4 · Ring-enhancing lesions that do not improve A patient with CD4 48, positive Toxoplasma IgG, and multiple lesions receives appropriate therapy but is unchanged at day 14. What should prevent automatic extension of empiric therapy? Discuss the next step Reassess exposure and adherence and pursue alternative diagnoses, particularly CNS lymphoma. Discuss biopsy. A presumptive toxoplasma diagnosis should have a defined reassessment point. [5] Case 5 · CMV PCR distracts from the involved organ A patient with CD4 19 has diarrhea and a positive plasma CMV PCR. Does this establish CMV colitis? Discuss the next step No. Obtain a syndrome-directed stool evaluation and consider endoscopy with biopsy. Ask about vision and arrange ophthalmology as indicated. Positive blood PCR does not by itself justify treatment for tissue disease. [18] Case 6 · Fever and cytopenias before MAC prophylaxis A patient newly diagnosed with HIV has CD4 12, fever, weight loss, cytopenias, and elevated alkaline phosphatase. Should weekly azithromycin be started immediately? Discuss the next step Evaluate active MAC and disseminated histoplasmosis, with appropriate cultures, antigen testing, and tissue when needed. MAC prophylaxis can expose active disease to monotherapy. Severe histoplasmosis warrants prompt amphotericin-based treatment. [17] [19] Case 7 · A suppressed patient wants fewer pills A patient with HIV/HBV is suppressed on tenofovir-containing ART and requests CAB/RPV. What cannot be lost in the switch? Discuss the next step HBV treatment. Review resistance and the rest of injectable eligibility, then preserve or separately provide appropriate HBV therapy. CAB/RPV itself does not treat HBV. [12] [36] Case 8 · A new exposure presents overnight An HIV-negative patient presents 18 hours after a substantial sexual exposure; the source result is pending. What action is time sensitive? Discuss the next step Start indicated PEP without waiting, obtain baseline testing, provide the full 28-day plan, and arrange follow-up and a PrEP transition discussion. [32]

slides.title: Discuss the next step
slides.section: Use these cases to practice a defensible next step
paragraphs: Evaluate active MAC and disseminated histoplasmosis, with appropriate cultures, antigen testing, and tissue when needed. MAC prophylaxis can expose active disease to monotherapy. Severe histoplasmosis warrants prompt amphotericin-based treatment. [17] [19]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Use these cases to practice a defensible next step Case 1 · An acute viral syndrome with discordant testing A 26-year-old has fever, rash, pharyngitis, a reactive antigen-antibody screen, and negative antibody differentiation. What is the next test, and what history changes empiric ART? Discuss the next step Obtain HIV RNA and ask about oral/injectable PrEP and PEP. Repeat an ambiguous result on a new specimen. If HIV followed CAB PrEP, request integrase genotype and use the recommended boosted-darunavir strategy while awaiting results. [1] Case 2 · New HIV with hypoxemic pneumonia A 42-year-old has CD4 38, diffuse ground-glass opacity, and room-air PaO₂ 62 mmHg. What should happen today, and when should ART begin? Discuss the next step Obtain respiratory PCP testing while starting treatment-dose TMP-SMX and adjunctive prednisone. Assess bacterial/TB coinfection and oxygen needs. Plan ART within 2 weeks and subsequent PCP prophylaxis. [6] Case 3 · Headache before rapid ART A 35-year-old with CD4 24 has 2 weeks of headache and a positive serum CrAg. Is same-day ART the next step? Discuss the next step First evaluate CNS disease with LP, including opening pressure and fungal culture, after imaging if indicated. Begin appropriate antifungals and manage pressure. CNS cryptococcosis usually calls for ART deferral around 4-6 weeks. [7] Case 4 · Ring-enhancing lesions that do not improve A patient with CD4 48, positive Toxoplasma IgG, and multiple lesions receives appropriate therapy but is unchanged at day 14. What should prevent automatic extension of empiric therapy? Discuss the next step Reassess exposure and adherence and pursue alternative diagnoses, particularly CNS lymphoma. Discuss biopsy. A presumptive toxoplasma diagnosis should have a defined reassessment point. [5] Case 5 · CMV PCR distracts from the involved organ A patient with CD4 19 has diarrhea and a positive plasma CMV PCR. Does this establish CMV colitis? Discuss the next step No. Obtain a syndrome-directed stool evaluation and consider endoscopy with biopsy. Ask about vision and arrange ophthalmology as indicated. Positive blood PCR does not by itself justify treatment for tissue disease. [18] Case 6 · Fever and cytopenias before MAC prophylaxis A patient newly diagnosed with HIV has CD4 12, fever, weight loss, cytopenias, and elevated alkaline phosphatase. Should weekly azithromycin be started immediately? Discuss the next step Evaluate active MAC and disseminated histoplasmosis, with appropriate cultures, antigen testing, and tissue when needed. MAC prophylaxis can expose active disease to monotherapy. Severe histoplasmosis warrants prompt amphotericin-based treatment. [17] [19] Case 7 · A suppressed patient wants fewer pills A patient with HIV/HBV is suppressed on tenofovir-containing ART and requests CAB/RPV. What cannot be lost in the switch? Discuss the next step HBV treatment. Review resistance and the rest of injectable eligibility, then preserve or separately provide appropriate HBV therapy. CAB/RPV itself does not treat HBV. [12] [36] Case 8 · A new exposure presents overnight An HIV-negative patient presents 18 hours after a substantial sexual exposure; the source result is pending. What action is time sensitive? Discuss the next step Start indicated PEP without waiting, obtain baseline testing, provide the full 28-day plan, and arrange follow-up and a PrEP transition discussion. [32]

slides.title: Case 8 · A new exposure presents overnight
slides.section: Use these cases to practice a defensible next step
paragraphs: An HIV-negative patient presents 18 hours after a substantial sexual exposure; the source result is pending.
What action is time sensitive?
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Use these cases to practice a defensible next step Case 1 · An acute viral syndrome with discordant testing A 26-year-old has fever, rash, pharyngitis, a reactive antigen-antibody screen, and negative antibody differentiation. What is the next test, and what history changes empiric ART? Discuss the next step Obtain HIV RNA and ask about oral/injectable PrEP and PEP. Repeat an ambiguous result on a new specimen. If HIV followed CAB PrEP, request integrase genotype and use the recommended boosted-darunavir strategy while awaiting results. [1] Case 2 · New HIV with hypoxemic pneumonia A 42-year-old has CD4 38, diffuse ground-glass opacity, and room-air PaO₂ 62 mmHg. What should happen today, and when should ART begin? Discuss the next step Obtain respiratory PCP testing while starting treatment-dose TMP-SMX and adjunctive prednisone. Assess bacterial/TB coinfection and oxygen needs. Plan ART within 2 weeks and subsequent PCP prophylaxis. [6] Case 3 · Headache before rapid ART A 35-year-old with CD4 24 has 2 weeks of headache and a positive serum CrAg. Is same-day ART the next step? Discuss the next step First evaluate CNS disease with LP, including opening pressure and fungal culture, after imaging if indicated. Begin appropriate antifungals and manage pressure. CNS cryptococcosis usually calls for ART deferral around 4-6 weeks. [7] Case 4 · Ring-enhancing lesions that do not improve A patient with CD4 48, positive Toxoplasma IgG, and multiple lesions receives appropriate therapy but is unchanged at day 14. What should prevent automatic extension of empiric therapy? Discuss the next step Reassess exposure and adherence and pursue alternative diagnoses, particularly CNS lymphoma. Discuss biopsy. A presumptive toxoplasma diagnosis should have a defined reassessment point. [5] Case 5 · CMV PCR distracts from the involved organ A patient with CD4 19 has diarrhea and a positive plasma CMV PCR. Does this establish CMV colitis? Discuss the next step No. Obtain a syndrome-directed stool evaluation and consider endoscopy with biopsy. Ask about vision and arrange ophthalmology as indicated. Positive blood PCR does not by itself justify treatment for tissue disease. [18] Case 6 · Fever and cytopenias before MAC prophylaxis A patient newly diagnosed with HIV has CD4 12, fever, weight loss, cytopenias, and elevated alkaline phosphatase. Should weekly azithromycin be started immediately? Discuss the next step Evaluate active MAC and disseminated histoplasmosis, with appropriate cultures, antigen testing, and tissue when needed. MAC prophylaxis can expose active disease to monotherapy. Severe histoplasmosis warrants prompt amphotericin-based treatment. [17] [19] Case 7 · A suppressed patient wants fewer pills A patient with HIV/HBV is suppressed on tenofovir-containing ART and requests CAB/RPV. What cannot be lost in the switch? Discuss the next step HBV treatment. Review resistance and the rest of injectable eligibility, then preserve or separately provide appropriate HBV therapy. CAB/RPV itself does not treat HBV. [12] [36] Case 8 · A new exposure presents overnight An HIV-negative patient presents 18 hours after a substantial sexual exposure; the source result is pending. What action is time sensitive? Discuss the next step Start indicated PEP without waiting, obtain baseline testing, provide the full 28-day plan, and arrange follow-up and a PrEP transition discussion. [32]

slides.title: Check the decision and explain why it is justified
slides.section: Check the decision and explain why it is justified
paragraphs: 1. Can a negative antigen-antibody test exclude acute HIV after a recent exposure?
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Check the decision and explain why it is justified 1. Can a negative antigen-antibody test exclude acute HIV after a recent exposure? Show explanation No. Obtain HIV RNA when the exposure and clinical syndrome justify concern; repeat testing as indicated. [1] 2. Can DTG/3TC be the default before HBV and genotype results? Show explanation No. Select a suitable rapid-start regimen with HBV activity while those results are pending. [8] 3. Does every patient with CD4 <50 need azithromycin prophylaxis? Show explanation No. Effective ART started immediately removes the routine indication; evaluate symptoms for active MAC before prophylaxis. [17] 4. What monitoring item is easy to miss with TMP-SMX? Show explanation Potassium, in addition to renal function, blood counts, rash, and other toxicity assessment. [6] 5. Does PCP prophylaxis have the same threshold in untreated and stably treated HIV? Show explanation No. For patients not on ART or starting ART, use CD4 <200. Restart decisions on ART incorporate CD4 and the viral-load pattern. [6] 6. Should ART start immediately for cryptococcal meningitis? Show explanation Usually no. Treat cryptococcosis and elevated intracranial pressure first; ART generally starts around 4-6 weeks. [7] 7. Does persistent CrAg mean induction has failed? Show explanation No. Follow clinical response, opening pressure, and CSF fungal cultures; antigen can persist. [7] 8. Can a negative plasma CMV PCR exclude CMV retinitis? Show explanation No. Retinal examination establishes the diagnosis in the appropriate clinical setting. [18] 9. Can a prevention lenacapavir injection treat established HIV by itself? Show explanation No. Treatment requires a fully active combination selected for treatment history and resistance. [39] 10. Does LATITUDE prove that all viremic patients should immediately receive CAB/RPV? Show explanation No. Randomization followed an initial supported oral phase and achievement of the trial viral-load threshold. Eligibility and implementation support matter. [38] 11. What is the definitive treatment principle for HIV-associated PML? Show explanation Rapid effective ART and immune restoration. There is no established JCV-specific antiviral regimen. [20] 12. What makes the discharge plan complete? Show explanation Medication supply through follow-up, a confirmed appointment, named ownership of pending results and toxicity monitoring, and clear return precautions. [2]

slides.title: Show explanation
slides.section: Check the decision and explain why it is justified
paragraphs: No. Obtain HIV RNA when the exposure and clinical syndrome justify concern; repeat testing as indicated. [1]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Check the decision and explain why it is justified 1. Can a negative antigen-antibody test exclude acute HIV after a recent exposure? Show explanation No. Obtain HIV RNA when the exposure and clinical syndrome justify concern; repeat testing as indicated. [1] 2. Can DTG/3TC be the default before HBV and genotype results? Show explanation No. Select a suitable rapid-start regimen with HBV activity while those results are pending. [8] 3. Does every patient with CD4 <50 need azithromycin prophylaxis? Show explanation No. Effective ART started immediately removes the routine indication; evaluate symptoms for active MAC before prophylaxis. [17] 4. What monitoring item is easy to miss with TMP-SMX? Show explanation Potassium, in addition to renal function, blood counts, rash, and other toxicity assessment. [6] 5. Does PCP prophylaxis have the same threshold in untreated and stably treated HIV? Show explanation No. For patients not on ART or starting ART, use CD4 <200. Restart decisions on ART incorporate CD4 and the viral-load pattern. [6] 6. Should ART start immediately for cryptococcal meningitis? Show explanation Usually no. Treat cryptococcosis and elevated intracranial pressure first; ART generally starts around 4-6 weeks. [7] 7. Does persistent CrAg mean induction has failed? Show explanation No. Follow clinical response, opening pressure, and CSF fungal cultures; antigen can persist. [7] 8. Can a negative plasma CMV PCR exclude CMV retinitis? Show explanation No. Retinal examination establishes the diagnosis in the appropriate clinical setting. [18] 9. Can a prevention lenacapavir injection treat established HIV by itself? Show explanation No. Treatment requires a fully active combination selected for treatment history and resistance. [39] 10. Does LATITUDE prove that all viremic patients should immediately receive CAB/RPV? Show explanation No. Randomization followed an initial supported oral phase and achievement of the trial viral-load threshold. Eligibility and implementation support matter. [38] 11. What is the definitive treatment principle for HIV-associated PML? Show explanation Rapid effective ART and immune restoration. There is no established JCV-specific antiviral regimen. [20] 12. What makes the discharge plan complete? Show explanation Medication supply through follow-up, a confirmed appointment, named ownership of pending results and toxicity monitoring, and clear return precautions. [2]

slides.title: Check the decision and explain why it is justified
slides.section: Check the decision and explain why it is justified
paragraphs: 3. Does every patient with CD4 <50 need azithromycin prophylaxis?
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Check the decision and explain why it is justified 1. Can a negative antigen-antibody test exclude acute HIV after a recent exposure? Show explanation No. Obtain HIV RNA when the exposure and clinical syndrome justify concern; repeat testing as indicated. [1] 2. Can DTG/3TC be the default before HBV and genotype results? Show explanation No. Select a suitable rapid-start regimen with HBV activity while those results are pending. [8] 3. Does every patient with CD4 <50 need azithromycin prophylaxis? Show explanation No. Effective ART started immediately removes the routine indication; evaluate symptoms for active MAC before prophylaxis. [17] 4. What monitoring item is easy to miss with TMP-SMX? Show explanation Potassium, in addition to renal function, blood counts, rash, and other toxicity assessment. [6] 5. Does PCP prophylaxis have the same threshold in untreated and stably treated HIV? Show explanation No. For patients not on ART or starting ART, use CD4 <200. Restart decisions on ART incorporate CD4 and the viral-load pattern. [6] 6. Should ART start immediately for cryptococcal meningitis? Show explanation Usually no. Treat cryptococcosis and elevated intracranial pressure first; ART generally starts around 4-6 weeks. [7] 7. Does persistent CrAg mean induction has failed? Show explanation No. Follow clinical response, opening pressure, and CSF fungal cultures; antigen can persist. [7] 8. Can a negative plasma CMV PCR exclude CMV retinitis? Show explanation No. Retinal examination establishes the diagnosis in the appropriate clinical setting. [18] 9. Can a prevention lenacapavir injection treat established HIV by itself? Show explanation No. Treatment requires a fully active combination selected for treatment history and resistance. [39] 10. Does LATITUDE prove that all viremic patients should immediately receive CAB/RPV? Show explanation No. Randomization followed an initial supported oral phase and achievement of the trial viral-load threshold. Eligibility and implementation support matter. [38] 11. What is the definitive treatment principle for HIV-associated PML? Show explanation Rapid effective ART and immune restoration. There is no established JCV-specific antiviral regimen. [20] 12. What makes the discharge plan complete? Show explanation Medication supply through follow-up, a confirmed appointment, named ownership of pending results and toxicity monitoring, and clear return precautions. [2]

slides.title: Show explanation
slides.section: Check the decision and explain why it is justified
paragraphs: Usually no. Treat cryptococcosis and elevated intracranial pressure first; ART generally starts around 4-6 weeks. [7]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Check the decision and explain why it is justified 1. Can a negative antigen-antibody test exclude acute HIV after a recent exposure? Show explanation No. Obtain HIV RNA when the exposure and clinical syndrome justify concern; repeat testing as indicated. [1] 2. Can DTG/3TC be the default before HBV and genotype results? Show explanation No. Select a suitable rapid-start regimen with HBV activity while those results are pending. [8] 3. Does every patient with CD4 <50 need azithromycin prophylaxis? Show explanation No. Effective ART started immediately removes the routine indication; evaluate symptoms for active MAC before prophylaxis. [17] 4. What monitoring item is easy to miss with TMP-SMX? Show explanation Potassium, in addition to renal function, blood counts, rash, and other toxicity assessment. [6] 5. Does PCP prophylaxis have the same threshold in untreated and stably treated HIV? Show explanation No. For patients not on ART or starting ART, use CD4 <200. Restart decisions on ART incorporate CD4 and the viral-load pattern. [6] 6. Should ART start immediately for cryptococcal meningitis? Show explanation Usually no. Treat cryptococcosis and elevated intracranial pressure first; ART generally starts around 4-6 weeks. [7] 7. Does persistent CrAg mean induction has failed? Show explanation No. Follow clinical response, opening pressure, and CSF fungal cultures; antigen can persist. [7] 8. Can a negative plasma CMV PCR exclude CMV retinitis? Show explanation No. Retinal examination establishes the diagnosis in the appropriate clinical setting. [18] 9. Can a prevention lenacapavir injection treat established HIV by itself? Show explanation No. Treatment requires a fully active combination selected for treatment history and resistance. [39] 10. Does LATITUDE prove that all viremic patients should immediately receive CAB/RPV? Show explanation No. Randomization followed an initial supported oral phase and achievement of the trial viral-load threshold. Eligibility and implementation support matter. [38] 11. What is the definitive treatment principle for HIV-associated PML? Show explanation Rapid effective ART and immune restoration. There is no established JCV-specific antiviral regimen. [20] 12. What makes the discharge plan complete? Show explanation Medication supply through follow-up, a confirmed appointment, named ownership of pending results and toxicity monitoring, and clear return precautions. [2]

slides.title: Check the decision and explain why it is justified
slides.section: Check the decision and explain why it is justified
paragraphs: 8. Can a negative plasma CMV PCR exclude CMV retinitis?
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Check the decision and explain why it is justified 1. Can a negative antigen-antibody test exclude acute HIV after a recent exposure? Show explanation No. Obtain HIV RNA when the exposure and clinical syndrome justify concern; repeat testing as indicated. [1] 2. Can DTG/3TC be the default before HBV and genotype results? Show explanation No. Select a suitable rapid-start regimen with HBV activity while those results are pending. [8] 3. Does every patient with CD4 <50 need azithromycin prophylaxis? Show explanation No. Effective ART started immediately removes the routine indication; evaluate symptoms for active MAC before prophylaxis. [17] 4. What monitoring item is easy to miss with TMP-SMX? Show explanation Potassium, in addition to renal function, blood counts, rash, and other toxicity assessment. [6] 5. Does PCP prophylaxis have the same threshold in untreated and stably treated HIV? Show explanation No. For patients not on ART or starting ART, use CD4 <200. Restart decisions on ART incorporate CD4 and the viral-load pattern. [6] 6. Should ART start immediately for cryptococcal meningitis? Show explanation Usually no. Treat cryptococcosis and elevated intracranial pressure first; ART generally starts around 4-6 weeks. [7] 7. Does persistent CrAg mean induction has failed? Show explanation No. Follow clinical response, opening pressure, and CSF fungal cultures; antigen can persist. [7] 8. Can a negative plasma CMV PCR exclude CMV retinitis? Show explanation No. Retinal examination establishes the diagnosis in the appropriate clinical setting. [18] 9. Can a prevention lenacapavir injection treat established HIV by itself? Show explanation No. Treatment requires a fully active combination selected for treatment history and resistance. [39] 10. Does LATITUDE prove that all viremic patients should immediately receive CAB/RPV? Show explanation No. Randomization followed an initial supported oral phase and achievement of the trial viral-load threshold. Eligibility and implementation support matter. [38] 11. What is the definitive treatment principle for HIV-associated PML? Show explanation Rapid effective ART and immune restoration. There is no established JCV-specific antiviral regimen. [20] 12. What makes the discharge plan complete? Show explanation Medication supply through follow-up, a confirmed appointment, named ownership of pending results and toxicity monitoring, and clear return precautions. [2]

Complete source section:
Check the decision and explain why it is justified 1. Can a negative antigen-antibody test exclude acute HIV after a recent exposure? Show explanation No. Obtain HIV RNA when the exposure and clinical syndrome justify concern; repeat testing as indicated. [1] 2. Can DTG/3TC be the default before HBV and genotype results? Show explanation No. Select a suitable rapid-start regimen with HBV activity while those results are pending. [8] 3. Does every patient with CD4 <50 need azithromycin prophylaxis? Show explanation No. Effective ART started immediately removes the routine indication; evaluate symptoms for active MAC before prophylaxis. [17] 4. What monitoring item is easy to miss with TMP-SMX? Show explanation Potassium, in addition to renal function, blood counts, rash, and other toxicity assessment. [6] 5. Does PCP prophylaxis have the same threshold in untreated and stably treated HIV? paragraphs: Teaching companion · September 21, 2026 · Faculty/local review pending. Use the full module for dosing, eligibility, evidence, and exceptions.
Ag/Ab → differentiation → RNA for discordance. Suspected acute HIV can need RNA despite a negative screen. Obtain CD4, RNA, genotype, organ function, HBV/HCV, and prior ART/PrEP history.

slides.notes:
Complete source section:
HIV and OIs · One-page rounds summary Teaching companion · September 21, 2026 · Faculty/local review pending. Use the full module for dosing, eligibility, evidence, and exceptions. Confirm and stage Ag/Ab → differentiation → RNA for discordance. Suspected acute HIV can need RNA despite a negative screen. Obtain CD4, RNA, genotype, organ function, HBV/HCV, and prior ART/PrEP history. Start appropriate ART Most: BIC/FTC/TAF or DTG + two NRTIs. Do not rapid-start DTG/3TC before HBV/genotype results. Prior CAB PrEP needs integrase genotype and an appropriate interim regimen. Preserve HBV treatment. Recognize the OI Pneumonia: PCP, bacteria, TB. Headache: CrAg/CSF with opening pressure. Focal deficit: MRI, toxoplasma/lymphoma/PML differential. Visual symptoms: urgent ophthalmology. Fever/cytopenias: MAC, histoplasmosis, TB, malignancy. Match ART timing to disease PCP: within 2 weeks. Cryptococcal meningitis: generally 4-6 weeks. TB without meningitis: within 2 weeks if CD4 <50; 2-8 weeks otherwise. TB meningitis: individualized guideline-informed plan. PML: immediate effective ART. Prescribe prevention correctly PCP: CD4 <200 if not on or starting ART. Toxoplasma: IgG+ and CD4 <100. MAC prophylaxis usually unnecessary with immediate effective ART; exclude active disease first. Secondary suppression has organism-specific stopping criteria. Monitor and hand off TMP-SMX: K+, creatinine, CBC. Amphotericin: renal function, K+/Mg. Flucytosine: CBC, renal adjustment/levels. Check interactions and absorption. Repeat HIV RNA at 4-8 weeks. Confirm medication supply, appointment, and result ownership. Use prevention opportunities Substantial exposure: indicated PEP immediately, no later than 72 hours, for 28 days. Arrange follow-up and PrEP transition. PrEP options include oral agents, CAB, and six-monthly LEN. Sustained suppression prevents sexual HIV transmission. Know when to reconsider No toxoplasma improvement by 10-14 days, new visual loss, rising oxygen need, persistent cultures, or new CNS symptoms require reassessment. Positive CMV blood PCR is not tissue disease; persistent CrAg is not proof of failure.

MAC prophylaxis usually unnecessary with immediate effective ART; exclude active disease first. Secondary suppression has organism-specific stopping criteria. Monitor and hand off TMP-SMX: K+, creatinine, CBC. Amphotericin: renal function, K+/Mg. Flucytosine: CBC, renal adjustment/levels. Check interactions and absorption. Repeat HIV RNA at 4-8 weeks. Arrange follow-up and PrEP transition. PrEP options include oral agents, CAB, and six-monthly LEN. Sustained suppression prevents sexual HIV transmission.
